The statement is true.

Complete equity financing is unrealistic for many businesses; debt capital often remains necessary.

The statement is false.

title: Debt capital from third parties
context: Evaluate the following statements on debt capital:
statements: If the capital comes from third parties, for example from a bank, it is called debt capital.
Debt capital is as a rule available only for a limited time and must be repaid.
Loans are the most essential form of debt capital.
Debt capital providers as a rule have the same say in company management as equity providers.
Interest usually need not be paid on debt capital, because only equity capital bears interest.
tactical_explanations:
Third parties supply outside funds. As soon as the capital does not come from founders or shareholders but from outside, for example from a bank, it is called debt capital. The bank becomes a creditor, not a co-owner by virtue of the loan; say in management as a rule remains absent. Suppliers can play the same role short-term when payment is on account. The designation follows the source "third parties", not the mere fact that money sits in the account. Repayment and usually interest belong to this relationship, in contrast to a contribution. The statement hits the definition of outside funds.

The statement is true.

Time limit and repayment belong to debt capital. It is ordinarily available only for a limited time and must be repaid. At the end of the term the capital itself must be returned, in addition to any interest. Equity capital does not know this repayment obligation. "Ordinarily" leaves special cases open but describes the standard the feature table records: short- or long-term depending on the agreement, always with repayment.

The statement is true.

The loan is the main form, not the only one. Loans are called the most essential form of debt capital. Long-term, banks in particular grant credit; short-term, suppliers with payment terms are added; large companies can issue bonds. The primacy of the loan does not erase these other routes but ranks them by frequency. Anyone who treats the loan as a marginal phenomenon misses the weighting of the account.

The statement is true.

Say follows legal status, not the amount of money. Equity providers have rights of say depending on the legal form; debt capital providers as a rule have no say in company management. A bank does not steer the business merely because it grants a loan, unless special security agreements provide otherwise. Equating both forms of say is the reverse of the table. Creditors secure repayment; shareholders manage.

The statement is false.

Interest typically sits on the debt side. Usually debt capital must bear interest, i.e. interest payments to creditors. Equity capital precisely does not demand such interest in loss years. The claim that debt capital is never to be interest-bearing and only equity capital carries interest reverses both columns of the table. Even those who pay on account and forgo cash discount are, strictly speaking, paying for the supplier credit. Freedom from interest is the exception here, not the rule.

The statement is false.

title: Equity and debt capital: say, security, term
context: Evaluate the following statements on the typical features of equity and debt capital:
statements: Equity providers have rights of say to differing degrees depending on the legal form.
Debt capital providers as a rule have no say in company management.
Debt capital as a rule need neither bear interest nor be repaid as long as the company earns profits.
If the loan is sufficiently secured, debt capital providers can have security for repayment.
Debt capital can, by agreement, be available short-term or long-term.
tactical_explanations:
Legal form governs the voice of the owners. Equity providers have rights of say, but not of uniform strength: the extent depends on the legal form. In a partnership different participation rules apply than in a capital company with management and shareholders' meeting. Differing does not mean arbitrarily zero; it means the form determines how far who has a say. Debt capital providers as a rule remain outside.

The statement is true.

Creditors as a rule do not run the business. Debt capital providers supply time-limited funds, demand interest and repayment, but do not sit in management in place of the shareholders. "As a rule" leaves special contractual bindings open but does not change the basic rule. Anyone who attributes to the bank the same influence as the owners mixes loan contract and shareholder status. Say typically remains with the owners.

The statement is true.

Debt capital is typically time-limited, repayable and interest-bearing — independent of profit phases.

The statement is false.

Security decides on the debt side. If the loan is sufficiently secured, debt capital providers can have security for repayment. Mortgage, pledge or comparable securities give access if payment is not made. Without adequate security this protection is lacking. The statement makes the conditionality clear and does not claim automatic full security for every loan.

The statement is true.

Agreement sets the term. Debt capital can be available short-term or long-term, depending on the contract. Trade payables often cover weeks, bank loans years, bonds likewise longer terms. Equity capital as a rule remains indefinite; the debt side is precisely the flexible one. Anyone who thinks of debt capital only as always long-term or only as always short-term ignores contractual freedom.

The statement is true.

title: Trade payables and cash discount (Skonto)
context: A trading business buys goods on account and considers whether to use cash discount (Skonto) or to stretch the payment term. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: In short-term credit financing, suppliers as well as banks are important lenders.
If deliveries need not be paid immediately but on account, financing is provided by the suppliers and trade payables arise.
If one forgoes a possible price deduction for immediate payment (Skonto) in order to use the payment term, interest is, strictly speaking, also being paid for paying on account.
The effective interest rate of the cash discount is in most cases so low that payment on account should be preferred.
Temporarily overdrawing the bank account in order to pay faster and use cash discount can be the economically more sensible option.
tactical_explanations:
Short-term credit has two typical providers. Long-term loan financing comes mainly from banks; short-term, suppliers stand alongside the banks. Anyone who thinks only of the institution around the corner as lender overlooks the payment term as a credit relationship with trade payables. The goods are there, the money not yet: that is exactly short-term debt capital, often without a separate loan contract. Forgone cash discount even makes it an expensive variant. The statement places both providers side by side, as the short-term side is described.

The statement is true.

On account means supplier financing. If payment comes later, the supplier finances the interval; in accounting terms, trade payables to these suppliers arise. That is not a gift and not equity capital, but short-term debt capital. The wording "on account" expressly translates as payment at a later date. Without this shift the business would have to deploy liquid funds immediately.

The statement is true.

Forgone cash discount is interest in another shape. Anyone who leaves the price deduction for immediate payment unused pays for the payment term: the higher invoice amount is the consideration for paying later. Strictly speaking, interest is therefore also being paid for paying on account. Supplier credit is not interest-free merely because no separate interest invoice arrives. Forgoing Skonto and loan interest are economically related.

The statement is true.

High, not low, is the typical effective interest rate. In most cases the effective interest rate of the cash discount is very high. Stretching the term can therefore be more expensive than a short overdraft. The recommendation always to pay on account because the Skonto effect is low reverses the order of magnitude. "In most cases very high" is the statement, not a side note. Anyone who treats the term as free deferral underestimates the cost.

The statement is false.

Overdraft can be cheaper than forgoing Skonto. Because the effective interest rate of the cash discount is often very high, temporarily overdrawing the bank account for faster payment can be the economically more sensible option. The business pays the bank interest for a few days and keeps the price deduction. That is not a plea for permanent overdraft, but a comparison of two short-term debt-capital costs. The statement reproduces exactly this trade-off.

Note: Skonto acts like expensive supplier credit, even without a stated interest rate.

The statement is true.

title: Internal financing and self-financing
context: Evaluate the following statements on internal financing:
statements: If the financing source stems from the company's sales, one speaks of internal financing.
Retaining profits is an important financing source, is also called self-financing, and increases equity capital.
Self-financing is external financing, because customers pay the consideration from outside the company.
Depreciation and the formation of provisions can also be a source of internal financing.
Internal financing exists only when a bank grants the company a loan that is later serviced from sales.
tactical_explanations:
Source in sales, name internal financing. The account separates by where the funds come from: from the company's sales or from outside. If the source lies in sales, the process is called internal financing. Sales proceeds feed self-financing through retained profits, as well as earned depreciation and provision effects, because expense arises there without outflow. The definition hangs on the source, not on the legal-form label and not on the fact that customers transfer money. Anyone who confuses internal financing with something inside the building or with a bank loan later repaid from sales misses the sales link of the source itself.

The statement is true.

Retention has a second name and a capital effect. Holding back profits is an important internal source, is called self-financing and increases equity capital. Less dependence on creditors, no debt-capital interest on these funds, a buffer against losses: exactly that is why it makes the company more crisis-resilient. Distribution would be the opposite path. The statement links designation and effect as the foundation links them.

The statement is true.

Customer payment does not turn profit into external financing. External financing exists when the source lies outside the company: new contributions, loans, bonds. That customers transfer the consideration is the sales from which internal financing stems. If every customer payment meant external financing, internal financing would not exist. Self-financing remains internal financing and an equity increase, not an inflow from outside in the sense of the diagram.

The statement is false.

Three internal paths stand side by side. Alongside retaining profits, depreciation and provisions can be sources of internal financing. Both reduce profit as expense without paying out at that moment; the funds remain in the business for the time being and can support other investments. Business logic expressly links them to internal financing. Anyone who allows only self-financing erases two of the named forms.

The statement is true.

A bank loan is external financing with debt capital. The source lies outside, with the bank as a third party. That repayment later comes from sales does not change the origin of the funds raised. Internal financing requires that the financing source itself stems from sales, not that an outside loan is eventually earned. The restriction "only when the bank..." reverses the definition.

The statement is false.

title: Retained profits and over-indebtedness
context: Evaluate the following statements on why retained profits make a company more crisis-resilient:
statements: Through self-financing the company is less dependent on debt capital providers.
No debt-capital interest need be paid on retained profits.
If substantial equity capital is present, a company can also survive several years of losses without being over-indebted.
If equity capital is quickly exhausted and debt capital exceeds assets, the company is over-indebted and economically at risk.
Self-financing through retained profits increases debt capital and dependence on creditors.
tactical_explanations:
Less creditor leverage follows from more own funds. Self-financing increases equity capital; the company then depends less on debt capital providers. Loans can still remain, but the share and the dependence fall if profits are not distributed but retained. Crisis resilience here means: not every investment step needs a new bank approval, and loss years first consume the own base rather than immediately the threshold of over-indebtedness. The statement reproduces the first of the named reasons, alongside freedom from interest, loss buffer and reinvestment in assets.

The statement is true.

Own funds carry no loan interest. Retained profits are equity capital, not an interest-bearing debt. Therefore no debt-capital interest need be paid for them. That eases the burden in years without profit, when a loan would still demand interest. Freedom from interest applies to this internal source, not to parallel bank loans. The second crisis point of the account is exactly this missing interest burden.

The statement is true.

The buffer against loss years is equity capital. Losses reduce equity capital. If much of it is present, several years of deficit can be absorbed without the company being over-indebted. The stock cushions the consumption. Thin equity would be exhausted after a short time. The statement describes this time buffer without trivialising losses.

The statement is true.

Over-indebtedness has a clear threshold. When equity capital is quickly exhausted and debt capital exceeds assets, the company is over-indebted and economically at risk. Debts larger than assets: the own base is gone. Exactly that is why substantial equity capital strengthens resilience. The statement is the counter-check to the loss buffer, not a second definition of insolvency proceedings.

The statement is true.

Retained profits increase equity capital and reduce dependence on debt capital providers.

The statement is false.

title: Depreciation financing
context: A business has invested 200,000 euros in tangible assets in one year, which are used for ten years. Evaluate the following statements on depreciation financing:
statements: If a company also includes the loss in value of machinery, computers and vehicles among its expenses, this loss in value is called depreciation.
Depreciation constitutes an outflow, so that the money leaves the company at the moment of booking.
Earned depreciation can in the meantime be used for other investments.
If the tangible assets are used for ten years, depreciation in this example amounts to 20,000 euros per year.
If the products are sold at the calculated prices, 200,000 euros from this depreciation are available every year for ten years.
tactical_explanations:
Loss in value has a name. In price formation the business takes account of all production expenses, usually plus profit. Expense includes the loss in value of machinery, computers, vehicles: that is depreciation. If sales are made at the calculated prices, this expense too is earned, although in the booking year no outflow equal to the loss in value leaves. Exactly that creates the internal-financing room for other investments — in the example 20,000 euros annually with a 200,000-euro acquisition and ten years of use. The statement names the term as the account introduces it, without confusing depreciation with the original purchase outflow.

The statement is true.

Booking is not outflow. The loss in value does not constitute an outflow; the money remains in the company for the time being. Exactly therein lies the financing effect: expense reduces profit, but the amount does not leave the till. Anyone who treats depreciation like a transfer to the machine dealer in the booking year confuses acquisition outflow and later allocation of the loss in value. The internal source arises because nothing is paid out.

The statement is false.

Park and redeploy. Because earned depreciation does not flow out, the funds can in the meantime be used for other investments. Operating assets thus stay current instead of the full acquisition amount lying idle until the replacement year. That is depreciation financing as internal financing, not a second equity contribution from shareholders. The statement hits the stated purpose of use.

The statement is true.

Acquisition divided by useful life. 200,000 euros in one year, use for ten years: 200,000 divided by 10 yields 20,000 euros depreciation per year. This amount enters prices like other costs. The division is the linear allocation of the example, not a new number invention. Anyone who books 200,000 every year as depreciation would want to earn the same purchase ten times.

The statement is true.

Annually 20,000 euros are available, not 200,000. If the goods are sold at the calculated prices, 20,000 euros are available every year for ten years. The 200,000 are the one-off acquisition, not the annual internal-financing amount. Anyone who expects the full investment sum as a depreciation inflow every year multiplies the example by ten. The identity is: acquisition 200,000, duration 10, annual amount 20,000.

The statement is false.

title: Provision financing
context: Evaluate the following statements on provision financing:
statements: Companies form provisions for possible future expenses and thus provide for them in the accounts.
Provisions can among other things concern a possible court case, holiday entitlements, pensions or Abfertigung payments.
Forming a provision constitutes an expense that reduces profit but is not an outflow.
Because a provision reduces profit, no funds are available in the meantime for other investments.
Pension provisions for employees who will only retire in 20 or 30 years can have a long-term financing effect.
tactical_explanations:
Provision is the core of the provision (Rückstellung). For possible future expenses, provision is made in the accounts before the amount flows. The company recognises the impending expense early instead of reacting only on the payout day. Internal financing arises because formation is expense without immediate outflow of funds, analogous to depreciation. Court risk, holiday, pension and Abfertigung are typical occasions; with pensions in 20 or 30 years the effect even becomes long-term. The statement reproduces the definition without already claiming that the money has already flowed to creditors.

The statement is true.

Four occasions are expressly named. A court case the company might lose, holiday entitlements, pensions and Abfertigung payments are named cases. The list is illustrative, not closed, but hits exactly the named types. Anyone who thinks of provisions only as a tax trick without substantive basis misses these occasions. Each case is a possible later expense for which booking is made now.

The statement is true.

Profit down, till still there. Formation is expense and lowers profit, similar to depreciation, without outflow. Liquidity that would otherwise appear as profit and perhaps be distributed therefore remains in the company. Creditors of a later pension have not yet received the money; the business can deploy the funds in the meantime. The statement separates profit effect and payment effect as the foundation does.

The statement is true.

Reducing profit does not lock the funds. Precisely because nothing is paid out, the amounts are available in the meantime for other investments. That is the financing effect, analogous to depreciation. The claim that after profit reduction nothing more is usable confuses accounting expense with an outflow from the account. Internal financing through provisions lives from this difference.

The statement is false.

Long horizons extend the effect. If employees only retire in 20 or 30 years, a wide interval lies between formation and payout. That is called a long-term financing effect. Short-term holiday provisions act for a shorter time; pensions carry for years. The statement takes over the numerical example of the account as a time horizon, not as a mandatory quota.

The statement is true.

title: External financing with equity and debt capital
context: Evaluate the following statements on external financing:
statements: If the financing source lies outside the company, one speaks of external financing.
From outside, both equity capital and debt capital can be supplied.
External financing consists only of debt capital, because new equity capital cannot be supplied from outside.
The most important debt capital providers from outside are, as previously set out, suppliers and banks.
Retaining profits from sales is the most important form of external financing.
tactical_explanations:
Outside means the source, not the building. If the financing source lies outside the company, the process is called external financing. New shareholder contributions — i.e. equity capital from existing or new participants — bank loans, trade payables and bond issues come from there. The opposite is sales as an internal source with self-financing, depreciation and provisions. Anyone who confuses outside with export markets or with the mere location of the machine misses the financial distinction. The statement is the definition and the entry into the overview.

The statement is true.

Two capital types from outside. The diagram and business logic say expressly: from outside, equity and debt capital can be supplied. Existing or new shareholders bring equity capital; banks, suppliers and bond creditors bring debt capital. External financing is therefore not a synonym for loan. Anyone who allows only one of the two sides halves the overview. The statement holds the dual assignment.

The statement is true.

From outside, equity and debt capital can come — e.g. new shareholders or loans.

The statement is false.

Suppliers and banks remain the main creditors. Business logic refers back: the most important debt capital providers are suppliers and banks. Short-term payment terms, short- and long-term loans; large businesses additionally bonds. The ranking does not exclude the bond but places everyday providers first. The statement repeats this weighting.

The statement is true.

Retention belongs inward. Self-financing stems from sales, increases equity capital and is internal financing. External financing would be a new contribution or a loan from third parties. Renaming profit retention as the most important external form mixes the two grids. Customers pay for performance; that does not make retained profit an inflow from capital providers outside in the sense of the diagram.

The statement is false.

title: Capital contributions and share issues
context: Evaluate the following statements on external financing by shareholders of a GmbH and of an Aktiengesellschaft:
statements: Shareholders of a GmbH must make contributions called Stammeinlagen or Geschäftsanteile.
The Stammeinlagen of different shareholders must be equal in amount, and a minimum share capital does not apply.
In an Aktiengesellschaft the share capital is divided into shares, so that large capital amounts can be raised more easily.
When shares are issued by the Aktiengesellschaft and bought by persons, this issue has a financing effect for the AG.
In share trading among shareholders a new financing effect regularly arises for the AG in the amount of the capital gain.
tactical_explanations:
GmbH contributions have two names. Shareholders must make contributions — Stammeinlagen or Geschäftsanteile. That is external financing with equity capital: the funds come from the participants, not from retained sales and not as a bank loan. Differing amounts are possible as long as overall the minimum share capital is reached; equality of each individual contribution is not required. The AG later divides share capital into shares; that does not change the GmbH terms. The statement hits designation and duty of GmbH shareholders without already mixing issue and share trading.

The statement is true.

Unequal and with a lower bound. The Stammeinlagen of different shareholders can differ in amount; overall, however, the minimum share capital must be reached. Equality of each contribution is not prescribed; the minimum share capital does indeed exist. The statement asserts the opposite of both rules. Anyone who demands equal mini-contributions without a lower bound does not describe the GmbH of the account.

The statement is false.

Division facilitates large amounts. The share capital, also called Aktienkapital, is divided into shares so that large capital amounts can be raised more easily. Many persons buy pieces instead of one single huge contribution. That is the financial point of the AG here, not primarily stock-exchange prestige. The statement reproduces exactly this raising effect.

The statement is true.

Issue brings funds; later trading does not. If the AG issues shares and persons buy them, capital flows to the AG: the financing effect of the issue. The share certifies a participation right in the share capital. Indefinite, without planned repayment to the shareholders. The statement describes only this first step, which business logic separates from later share trading.

The statement is true.

Trading in existing shares among investors brings the AG no additional inflow of funds.

The statement is false.

title: Share trading, price and capital increase
context: Evaluate the following statements on share trading and capital increase:
statements: Repayment of the share capital to the shareholders is not provided for; it is capital made available indefinitely.
If a shareholder sells her shares to another person, a further financing effect arises for the Aktiengesellschaft in the same amount as at the issue.
Shareholders benefit from capital gains in share trading.
If an Aktiengesellschaft increases its share capital, existing shareholders initially have the right to buy the newly issued young shares.
Anyone who sells the subscription right to young shares thereby prevents other persons from becoming shareholders.
tactical_explanations:
Indefinite and without a repayment plan. Share capital is not to be repaid to the shareholders; it is available indefinitely, matching the equity side of the feature table. Shareholders exit by selling holdings to others, not by the AG redeeming share capital like a loan. This sale creates no further financing effect for the company, in contrast to the issue. The statement holds exactly this duration of the contribution. Redemption at nominal would be the vocabulary of the bond as debt capital, not of the share as a participation right.

The statement is true.

The secondary market does not feed the AG. Through share trading no further financing effect arises for the AG. Money changes hands between old and new participants; the company's share capital remains the same. Only the issue — sale by the AG itself — brings it funds. Equating onward sale and issue wrongly doubles the inflow. Capital gains go to the selling shareholders.

Note: Only issuance by the AG finances the company, not trading among investors.

The statement is false.

Capital gain stays with the shareholders. Anyone who sells dearer than they bought realises the difference; the AG does not receive this amount on the secondary sale. Business logic separates clearly: no further financing effect for the AG; shareholders benefit from capital gains. Supply and demand set the price. The statement hits the assignment of the advantage.

The statement is true.

Subscription rights protect the quota. On a capital increase, existing shareholders may first buy the young shares and thus keep their percentage share of the share capital if they wish. The right follows from shareholder status, not from a stock-exchange whim. Anyone who ignores the young shares dilutes their holding if others subscribe. The statement reproduces the first stage of the increase.

The statement is true.

Sale of the subscription right opens the door instead of closing it. Anyone who sells the subscription right enables others to buy shares and become new shareholders. It is expressly stated as an alternative to buying oneself. Preventing that would precisely mean holding on and subscribing oneself. The claim reverses the effect of the sale.

The statement is false.

title: Bonds as debt capital
context: Evaluate the following statements on financing via bonds:
statements: Large companies have the option of raising debt capital by issuing a bond.
Bonds are also called Schuldverschreibungen, Renten or Bonds and are securities that certify a claim right.
The bond nominal can be divided into smaller partial amounts (denominated), so that many lenders can provide partial amounts.
Bonds certify a participation right in the share capital — comparable to shares.
Bond creditors earn interest according to the coupon and, if they sell before maturity, the difference between purchase and sale price.
tactical_explanations:
Issue instead of a single giant loan. Large companies can raise debt capital by issuing a bond, because especially large amounts are hard to obtain as a loan from one bank. The Austrian state appears as a further large debtor alongside, for example, voestalpine AG. Denomination divides the nominal so that many creditors subscribe partial amounts. The bond is external financing with debt capital and a claim right, not a second share issue with a participation right. Redemption at the end of the term remains the expectation. The statement hits possibility and capital type.

The statement is true.

Three bynames, one legal character. Schuldverschreibungen, Renten or Bonds are other words for bonds. They are securities that certify a claim right: the buyers have a claim against the issuer, a large debtor, on agreed terms of interest and term. That is the counterpart to the share with a participation right. The statement links names and legal content.

The statement is true.

Denomination opens many providers. The bond nominal — the large amount needed — is divided into smaller partial amounts. Many different lenders buy one or more parts. Thus what would be hard as a single bank loan becomes financeable. voestalpine AG and the Austrian state serve as an order of magnitude, not as mandatory issuers for every GmbH. The statement describes the technical core of denomination.

The statement is true.

Bonds certify a claim right; participation rights are shares.

The statement is false.

Two sources of return if not held to the end. Interest according to the coupon and, on sale before maturity, the difference between purchase and sale price. Anyone who holds to the due date receives redemption plus interest, not necessarily the same capital gain. The price during the term follows supply and demand. The statement names exactly the two listed returns.

The statement is true.

title: Bond interest, Euribor and floaters
context: Evaluate the following statements on bond terms and on Euribor:
statements: The interest rate is among the most important bond terms and can be fixed, i.e. unchanging, or variable during the term.
With variable interest, the rate is adjusted to the general interest-rate level, for example to Euribor.
Euribor means Euro Interbank Offered Rate and denotes average interest rates at which banks grant each other short-term euro deposits.
Variable-interest bonds are called so-called floaters.
The price of a bond is determined mainly by the nominal and hardly by supply and demand.
tactical_explanations:
The interest rule is the core of the terms. Interest, term and related agreements determine on what conditions the large debtor borrows money. Interest can remain fixed over the term or change. Fixed means unchanging; variable means adjustable to the general interest-rate level, for example via Euribor; such papers are called floaters. Anyone who knows only one of the two forms as the bond suppresses the other and also confuses price and nominal. The statement reproduces the alternative for the most important term without cancelling redemption at the end.

The statement is true.

Adjustment needs a reference. Variable means: the interest rate is adjusted to the general interest-rate level; as an example, Euribor is named. If the reference rate rises or falls, the bond interest moves with it. That affects creditors and issuer differently from a fixed coupon. The statement links variable and example index without forcing every contract onto Euribor.

The statement is true.

Banks among themselves, euro, short-term. Euribor is the Euro Interbank Offered Rate: average interest rates at which banks grant each other short-term euro deposits. There are different rates depending on the exact term. They serve as a base rate for financial transactions, including variable-interest bonds. The statement is the definition of the box, not stock-market wisdom outside the material.

The statement is true.

Floater is the name for the variable bond. Variable-interest bonds are called so-called floaters; Euribor can be their base rate. The nickname changes nothing about the character: still debt capital, still redemption at the end, only the interest side floats with the market. Anyone who takes floaters for shares because the name sounds English leaves the foundation. The statement equates designation and substance.

The statement is true.

The bond price is formed by supply and demand; the nominal is the repayment reference, not the current price.

The statement is false.

title: Equity, debt, internal and external
context: A Viennese manufacturing GmbH combines founders' contributions in kind, retained profits, trade payables, a bank loan and later a share issue after conversion into an AG. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: A bank loan is external financing with debt capital.
Self-financing through retained profits is internal financing and increases equity capital.
Founders' contributions in kind are debt capital, because a delivery van drives into the hall from outside.
Trade payables from paying on account are short-term debt capital, not equity capital.
Onward sale of already issued shares among investors is for the Aktiengesellschaft the same external financing as the issue.
tactical_explanations:
Two grids, one loan. The bank is a third party; the source lies outside: external financing. The capital must be repaid and usually bears interest; creditors without typical say: debt capital. Both at once, not either-or. Retained profits would be the counterpart internal and equity; founders' contributions in kind remain equity even if the delivery van rolls through the gate; trade payables are short-term debt. Only the issue newly feeds an AG, not later share trading. The statement correctly crosses the definitions at the most everyday example of the bank loan.

The statement is true.

Sales, retention, higher own base. The source is sales, hence internal financing; the form is called self-financing; the effect is more equity capital and more crisis resilience. No new creditors, no outside interest on this amount, a buffer against loss years. Anyone who reinterprets the same profit retention as a loan from customers slips into the external-debt corner that theory does not provide. The statement holds origin and capital type.

The statement is true.

Physically outside is not financially debt. Founders' contributions in kind increase equity capital: delivery vans and PCs count like money. External financing with equity capital would be conceivable if the contribution comes from shareholders, but never debt capital merely because the vehicle rolls through the gate. Debt capital comes from third parties as a credit relationship. Confusing physical location and capital quality is the trap.

The statement is false.

Payment terms create creditors, not shareholders. Paying on account means supplier financing and trade payables: short-term debt capital, often without a formal bank contract, with hidden interest via forgone Skonto. Equity capital would be a contribution or retained profit. Suppliers as a rule have no say in management. The statement places the position in the debt column and the short term.

The statement is true.

The issue feeds the AG; the secondary market does not. On the first sale by the company, capital flows in — external financing with equity capital. Thereafter investors exchange pieces; the AG receives no further financing effect; capital gains remain with the sellers. The same booking as at the issue does not exist on onward sale. Equating both processes is the hardest classification trap.

The statement is false.

title: How long are equity and debt capital available?
context: A company finances itself both through shareholder contributions and through a bank loan. Evaluate the following statements on the term of equity and debt capital:
statements: Equity capital is as a rule available to the company only for a limited time and must be repaid like a loan.
A bank loan with a ten-year term contradicts the rule that debt capital can be available short-term and long-term.
Whether debt capital is available short- or long-term depends on the agreement between the contracting parties, not on a uniform term.
Because equity capital is as a rule indefinite, it must nonetheless be repaid in full to the providers by a fixed end date.
A shareholder who can demand repayment of their contribution at any time on request fits the rule that equity capital is bound long-term.
tactical_explanations:
Equity capital is as a rule available indefinitely and need not be repaid — in contrast to debt capital.

The statement is false.

Ten years remain debt capital. A bank loan with a long term does not contradict the rule that debt capital can be short- or long-term; it precisely illustrates the long-term variant. Investment loans with multi-year terms are common. Only equity capital is as a rule considered indefinite. A long term does not change the assignment to debt capital.

The statement is false.

Neither weeks nor decades are prescribed for debt capital; what matters is what creditor and debtor agree. Trade payables run short; investment loans or bonds often over many years. This flexibility distinguishes debt capital from the as-a-rule indefinite equity binding.

The statement is true.

A repayment obligation at a fixed end date is precisely the feature of debt capital, not of equity capital. Because equity capital need not be repaid, it is suitable for long-term investments; a duty of full repayment would treat the contribution like a loan, which contradicts the rule.

The statement is false.

A right to demand the contribution back at any time on request resembles a short-term claim more than a long-term bound contribution. The rule describes equity capital precisely by its remaining bound as a rule indefinitely and not being withdrawable on call. An anytime recovery right would be the exception, not the rule.

The statement is false.

title: How are equity and debt capital providers remunerated?
context: The same company pays both profit shares to its shareholders and interest to its bank. Evaluate the following statements on the remuneration for equity and debt capital:
statements: Equity providers can receive profit shares but are not, in every year, dependent on fixed interest payments like creditors.
Anyone who repays a loan to the bank also at the same time repays the debt capital itself, in addition to the interest.
A shareholder has, similarly to a bank, a fixed agreed interest claim that must be paid independently of the company's annual result.
The duty to repay the capital employed at the end of the term concerns debt capital, not the contribution of the equity providers.
Because equity capital demands no fixed interest, it is for the company in bad years the more plannable and cheaper form of financing than debt capital.
tactical_explanations:
Profit shares to equity providers are possible but not mandatorily owed; if profit fails, distribution as a rule also fails. Creditors by contrast have an interest claim that in principle exists independently of business success. Exactly this difference keeps equity capital from being a fixed loan obligation.

The statement is true.

Interest and principal belong together. On debt capital, interest runs during the term, and at the end the capital itself must additionally be repaid. Anyone who counts only interest omits redemption of the loan sum. Both components form the repayment to the bank. Equity capital does not know this double duty in this form.

The statement is true.

A fixed interest claim independent of the annual result is accordingly typical for creditors, not for equity providers. Shareholders receive profit shares at most if and insofar as profit is earned; in loss years this claim fails. Equating that with fixed loan interest transfers creditor logic onto equity capital.

The statement is false.

Repayment duty hits the debt side. Debt capital must be repaid at the end of the term; the contribution of equity providers need not. Equity capital remains permanently available to the company so long as it is not consumed by losses. Anyone who attributes the same repayment duty to both sides erases the central difference.

The statement is true.

Without a fixed interest burden, equity capital remains more flexible. In weak years, fixed loan instalments strain liquidity more than a contribution without compulsory interest. Equity capital absorbs losses without interest and redemption additionally falling due. Exactly that is why it counts as a risk buffer compared with a fixed-interest loan. Plannability here means the absence of payment compulsion, not a higher return.

The statement is true.

title: Annual depreciation with linear allocation
context: A company buys tangible assets for 200,000 euros and plans a ten-year useful life, depreciated linearly. Evaluate the following statements on annual depreciation:
statements: Annual depreciation amounts to 200,000 euros divided by 10 years, i.e. 20,000 euros per year.
Because the residual book value falls from year to year, under linear depreciation the annual depreciation must also fall from year to year.
After one year the residual book value is 200,000 minus 20,000, i.e. 180,000 euros.
After two years cumulative depreciation amounts to 20,000 euros, because only the first year counts.
In every year of use the full acquisition amount of 200,000 euros is again available as depreciation.
tactical_explanations:
Evenly over ten years. Under linear depreciation the acquisition amount of 200,000 euros is allocated evenly over the useful life: 200,000 divided by 10 yields 20,000 euros per year. This amount remains constant over the entire useful life. There is no rising or falling annual rate in this model. The division is the entire annual logic.

The statement is true.

Linear means a constant annual amount, not falling annual depreciation. The residual book value does fall each year as already depreciated amounts accumulate, yet the annual depreciation itself remains equal at 20,000 euros. Falling annual depreciation would presuppose a different depreciation method.

The statement is false.

One annual amount reduces the opening value once. 200,000 minus 20,000 yields 180,000 euros residual book value after the first year of use. The residual book value arises directly from this subtraction without further assumptions. Nine annual amounts remain open. As long as linear and without residual value is used, the calculation stays this simple and stable.

The statement is true.

Two years mean two amounts. Cumulative depreciation after two years is 2 times 20,000 equals 40,000 euros, not 20,000. Anyone who counts only the first year ignores the second year of use, although the question expressly names two years. Cumulative means the sum of all previous annual amounts. A single year does not suffice for that.

The statement is false.

This point: the acquisition amount is allocated only once. Over ten years, ten times 20,000 euros are available in total, not 200,000 euros again every year. Anyone who repeats the full purchase price annually multiplies the actual acquisition by ten. Linear depreciation allocates the one amount; it does not multiply it. Annual depreciation remains 20,000 euros.

The statement is false.

title: Residual book value after several years of use
context: The same acquisition of 200,000 euros is depreciated linearly over ten years. Evaluate the following statements on the residual book value after several years of use:
statements: After five years the residual book value is half the acquisition value, i.e. 100,000 euros.
After five years only 20,000 euros have been cumulatively depreciated, because only the last annual amount counts.
After five years the residual book value is only 20,000 euros, because then only one annual amount would remain open.
After ten years the residual book value is zero if no residual value was agreed and depreciation is linear over the entire useful life.
The annual depreciation of 20,000 euros actually flows each year of use as a payment from the bank account.
tactical_explanations:
Halfway through useful life, half the book value. After five of ten years, 5 times 20,000 equals 100,000 euros have been depreciated; the residual book value is 200,000 minus 100,000 equals 100,000 euros. Under linear allocation without residual value, half the time corresponds exactly to half the acquisition value. The symmetry is therefore intentional here.

The statement is true.

Cumulative means the sum of all years. After five years, 5 times 20,000 equals 100,000 euros have been depreciated, not only the last annual amount of 20,000. The claim counts a single year instead of all five. The residual book value accordingly falls to 100,000 euros. Anyone who takes only the last amount massively underestimates the sum already allocated.

The statement is false.

After five years, five years remain open. Remaining useful life 5 times 20,000 yields 100,000 euros residual book value, not 20,000. A residual book value of 20,000 would arise only after nine years (200,000 minus 9 times 20,000). The statement confuses halfway through useful life with the penultimate year. Five years are not nine.

The statement is false.

At the end of useful life stands zero. After ten years the entire acquisition amount is accordingly allocated: 200,000 minus 10 times 20,000 equals 0 euros. Without an agreed residual value, nothing remains on the books for the asset. Linear allocation has then reached its goal. A positive residual book value would presuppose an expressly set residual value.

The statement is true.

Depreciation is accordingly an accounting expense, not an actual outflow. The money for the acquisition already flowed out in the year of purchase; the annual 20,000 euros thereafter only reduce profit without money again leaving the account in those years. Exactly therein lies the internal-financing effect of depreciation.

The statement is false.

title: Say and repayment security for equity and debt capital
context: Evaluate the following statements on who has a say with equity and debt capital and who receives security for repayment:
statements: How strongly equity providers may have a say depends on the legal form of the company and is therefore not equally strong everywhere.
Creditors who grant a company a loan as a rule have the same say in company management as the shareholders.
Equity providers basically have security for repayment of their contribution, similar to a secured bank loan.
A loan can be secured for the creditor, but need not be; security depends on whether the loan was sufficiently secured.
Because creditors are usually better secured than shareholders, they in return also have more say in company management.
tactical_explanations:
Legal form governs the strength of say. In a partnership different participation rules apply than in a GmbH or AG. Differently pronounced means not equally strong everywhere and not basically zero. Equity providers have a say, but the extent follows the form. Anyone who expects the same voice everywhere overlooks this gradation.

The statement is true.

A loan gives no shareholder voice. Creditors supply funds and demand interest and repayment, but as a rule do not sit in company management in place of the owners. Say and lending are separate matters. Anyone who attributes the same management rights to both mixes debt and equity capital. The bank remains a creditor.

The statement is false.

Without repayment duty, no repayment security. Equity capital need not be repaid; therefore there is basically no security for the contribution analogous to a secured bank loan. Security would only make sense with a repayment duty. The statement transfers debt-capital logic onto own funds and is therefore false.

The statement is false.

Security is accordingly negotiable, not automatic. Whether a loan is secured for the creditor depends on mortgage, pledge or comparable arrangements. Without adequate security this protection does not exist of itself. "If sufficiently secured" makes the conditionality clear. Debt capital can, but need not, be secured.

The statement is true.

Security does not buy say. Creditors can have their repayment secured but thereby receive no additional say in management. That as a rule remains with the equity providers, graded by legal form. Anyone who derives more management rights from better security links two independent features improperly.

The statement is false.

title: Financing features and depreciation examined together
context: A workshop finances new machines partly through shareholder contributions, partly through a bank loan. The same machines cost 200,000 euros and are depreciated linearly over ten years. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: A bank loan is debt capital: it bears interest, must be repaid, and as a rule gives the bank no say.
The workshop's shareholder contribution is equity capital: bound indefinitely, without repayment security, with say depending on legal form.
Annual depreciation of the machines turns them into debt capital once more than half their value has been depreciated.
After one year the residual book value of the machines is 180,000 euros; the retained depreciation nonetheless remains internal financing and not a loan.
Because equity capital is available indefinitely, annual depreciation of the machines must likewise amount to the full purchase price of 200,000 euros.
tactical_explanations:
A bank loan carries debt-capital features. It bears interest, must be repaid, and as a rule gives the bank no say. The bank remains a creditor, not a shareholder. Interest and repayment strain liquidity in a plannable way over the term. Exactly this combination distinguishes the loan from the shareholder contribution.

The statement is true.

The contribution carries equity-capital features. It is accordingly as a rule bound indefinitely, without security for repayment, with say depending on legal form. That is the counterpart to the bank loan. Losses can reduce the contribution without a repayment instalment falling due. The workshop thus finances itself permanently through owners' funds.

The statement is true.

Depreciation does not change the form of financing. Whether machines were bought with a contribution or a loan is decided by financing at the time of acquisition. The annual loss in value creates no new creditor and no repayment duty. Even when more than half has been depreciated, equity capital remains equity capital and debt capital remains debt capital. The statement mixes value consumption and capital origin.

The statement is false.

Residual book value falls; financing stays internal. 200,000 minus 20,000 yields 180,000 euros after one year. The 20,000 euros are expense without outflow; earned via the calculated prices, the money initially remains in the company. That is accordingly internal financing through earned depreciation, not a loan contract with a third party. Book value and financing source are to be separated.

The statement is true.

Indefinite equity capital does not govern the amount of depreciation. Depreciation follows useful life: 200,000 divided by 10 yields 20,000 euros per year, not 200,000 euros again every year. Anyone who mixes the term of the contribution with the pace of depreciation multiplies the purchase price by ten. Both topics belong to different calculation circles.

The statement is false.

title: Earned depreciation as a financing source
context: Depreciation of an acquisition of 200,000 euros over ten years enters the calculated selling prices. Evaluate the following statements on the financing effect:
statements: Annual depreciation remains equally high over the entire useful life as long as depreciation is linear.
If the products are sold at the calculated prices, depreciation is available to the company as a source of internal financing without money flowing out for it.
The financing effect of depreciation arises because as expense it reduces profit but in this step triggers no outflow.
After two years of use, 400,000 euros are already available as annual depreciation from this one acquisition.
If the residual book value of an asset falls, annual depreciation also doubles automatically.
tactical_explanations:
Linear means a constant annual amount. 200,000 divided by 10 yields 20,000 euros, equally high in each of the ten years of use. Only the residual book value falls year by year; annual depreciation itself remains unchanged. Declining-balance or usage-based models would be other allocations. Here the rate stays flat over the entire useful life.

The statement is true.

Earned depreciation stays internal. If companies build depreciation into selling prices and sell at those prices, they earn the amount through sales. At the same amount the money need not flow out again and is available as a source of internal financing. The prerequisite is accordingly sale at the calculated prices. Without sales the financing effect is missing.

The statement is true.

Expense without outflow is accordingly the lever. Depreciation reduces reported profit without money leaving the company in this booking step; the outflow for the asset already occurred in the year of acquisition. Exactly this mechanism explains depreciation financing. Anyone who equates expense with immediate outflow of money misses the time shift.

The statement is true.

Two years are 40,000, not 400,000. Cumulatively, 2 times 20,000 euros result. 400,000 would be twenty times the annual amount or twice the entire acquisition; neither is available. Anyone who confuses annual amount and acquisition value or multiplies wrongly by the year count lands at such fantasy sums.

The statement is false.

Residual book value and annual depreciation do not move in parallel under linear depreciation: the residual book value falls from year to year; annual depreciation remains constant at 20,000 euros. Doubling the annual amount would presuppose a different depreciation method not used here.

The statement is false.

title: Financing features and depreciation logic combined
context: Combine your knowledge of equity/debt capital and of linear depreciation of an acquisition of 200,000 euros over ten years. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: After five years of linear depreciation the residual book value is half the acquisition value.
Because the machines are depreciated over ten years, a loan to finance these machines may have a term of at most ten years.
After two years the residual book value is 160,000 euros if depreciation is linear over ten years.
Because equity providers have no repayment security, they must receive their contribution back at the latest at the end of the asset's depreciation period.
Annual depreciation is earned expense without outflow; after five years the half book value remains, not five times the original acquisition as a cash inflow.
tactical_explanations:
Halfway yields half the book value. Under linear depreciation over ten years, after five years 5 times 20,000 equals 100,000 euros have been allocated; the residual book value is 100,000 euros, i.e. half of 200,000. The symmetry holds as long as no residual value is agreed. Five of ten years are exactly the middle of useful life and thus also of value.

The statement is true.

An asset's useful life sets no upper limit on the loan term with which it is financed. Debt capital can by agreement be short- or long-term, independently of over how many years the related asset is depreciated. Both questions — depreciation period and loan term — are to be answered independently of each other.

The statement is false.

Two annual amounts reduce to 160,000. 200,000 minus 2 times 20,000 yields 160,000 euros residual book value. That lies between the value after one year (180,000) and that after five years (100,000). The calculation follows the same linear logic without residual value. Anyone who expects 160,000 has correctly subtracted two years of use from the acquisition value.

The statement is true.

Equity capital basically need not be repaid, independently of how long an asset financed with it is used or depreciated. The missing repayment security is accordingly precisely the expression of this missing repayment duty, not a deadline tied to the depreciation period.

The statement is false.

Five annual amounts summed, not multiplied by five. Cumulatively 100,000 euros have been depreciated; the residual book value falls to half. That is accordingly something other than a fivefold cash inflow of 1,000,000 euros, which does not exist here. Depreciation remains expense without outflow. Anyone who multiplies annual amounts by the purchase price invents an inflow.

The statement is true.

title: Areas of accounting
context: Assess the following statements on which questions business accounting answers:
statements: Financial accounting (financial planning, budgeting, cash flow) answers whether the company can manage with its financial resources or whether there is a financing need.
Bookkeeping with the balance sheet and the profit and loss statement answers what assets a company has, how those assets were financed, and whether a profit or a loss arose in a period.
Whether the company can manage with its financial resources is answered primarily by cost accounting.
Cost accounting asks how much the product manufactured or the service provided costs and how much the sales revenue contributes to covering costs.
Financial accounting, bookkeeping and cost accounting all answer the same single question, namely only that of annual profit.
tactical_explanations:
Three questions, three areas. Can the company manage with its financial resources, or is there a financing need? That is exactly what financial accounting answers — financial planning, budgeting and cash flow. Bookkeeping takes assets, financing and period result; cost accounting takes unit costs and cost coverage. Anyone who assigns liquidity and financing need to cost accounting swaps the table. The statement matches the book's assignment.

The statement is true.

Assets and financing stand side by side, plus the period result. What assets does the company have, how were they financed, and has it become richer or poorer in a given time — profit or loss? That is bookkeeping: preparing the balance sheet and the profit and loss statement. Financial accounting checks cash, not the asset structure. Cost accounting asks about product costs.

The statement is true.

Liquidity is not the cost question. Whether the company can manage with its financial resources or has a financing need sits in the table under financial accounting. Cost accounting asks how expensive the product or service is and what sales contribute to covering costs. Anyone who assigns the 'can we manage with our funds' question to cost accounting swaps the areas. A business can calculate cost-covering prices and still be insolvent if cash inflows and outflows diverge in time. The table deliberately separates these questions. The assignment stays tabularly separate; it is not freely interchangeable.

The statement is false.

Units and contribution, not account balance. How much does the product manufactured or the service provided cost, and how much does the revenue from the sale contribute to covering costs? That is cost accounting. Financial accounting checks inflows and outflows; bookkeeping checks assets and period result. The statement restates the third table row without cancelling the other areas.

The statement is true.

One profit figure does not replace three instruments. The table assigns the funds-and-financing question to financial accounting, assets, financing and period result to bookkeeping, and product costs and cost coverage to cost accounting. Anyone who claims all three areas answer only annual profit turns three questions into one and erases liquidity and costing. Profit appears in bookkeeping but replaces neither the financial plan nor cost accounting.

The statement is false.

title: Solvency and insolvency
context: Assess the following statements on the solvency of companies:
statements: A company must be solvent — that is, liquid — at all times.
Solvency means that all invoices due for investments and ongoing expenses can be paid.
If liquidity is no longer given, the company is at risk and insolvency threatens.
Unlike private households, companies do not need ongoing solvency because they can always wait for future profits.
To plan solvency, financial plans — that is, budgets — are prepared.
tactical_explanations:
Household and business share the same constraint. Just like private households, a company must be solvent at all times — liquid. It is not about a one-off check at the balance-sheet date, but about the ability to meet due obligations whenever they arise. Without this ongoing ability, continued existence is in question. The statement records exactly this requirement. Anyone who checks liquidity only at the balance-sheet date misses the ongoing nature of this duty.

The statement is true.

Due means payable, not planned sometime later. Solvency means that all invoices due for investments and ongoing expenses can be paid. A machine on paper or an expected annual profit does not replace the transfer. The statement links liquidity to concrete payments due now — what financial accounting steers. An invoice due only in months does not yet threaten today's liquidity; one due today does.

The statement is true.

Without liquidity the business tips over. If solvency is no longer given, the company is at risk; insolvency threatens. Business logic couples the absence of liquidity not to a mere image problem but to existence. Countermeasures and financial plans keep exactly this emergency in view. The statement restates the warning.

The statement is true.

Expected profit is not a means of payment. Companies and private households are expressly placed side by side: both must be liquid at all times. The claim that businesses can wait for future profits and therefore need no ongoing solvency erases exactly this parallel. Profit arises in bookkeeping via revenues and expenses; liquidity via cash inflows and outflows. Anyone who only looks to later profit may still be unable to settle due invoices. Then insolvency threatens, even if the P&L would later show black figures.

The statement is false.

Plan instead of hope. To plan solvency, financial plans are prepared; business logic also calls them budgets. Without matching planned cash inflows and outflows, liquidity remains chance. The statement names the instrument with which solvency is prepared.

The statement is true.

title: Structure of a financial plan
context: Assess the following statements on a company's financial plan:
statements: In principle, companies' financial plans resemble those of private households.
In the financial plan, planned cash inflows are set against planned cash outflows for a given period.
The financial plan sets period profit against depreciation, not cash inflows and outflows.
If a shortfall results, that means a financing need.
A period of about one month, for example, can be used for this comparison.
tactical_explanations:
Same principle, different scale. Companies' financial plans resemble those of private households in principle: planned inflows and planned outflows are compared for a period. The items are called cash inflows and cash outflows; the pattern stays household-like. Anyone who presents the company financial plan as a completely different logic contradicts this starting point. Size and legal form do not change the principle; they only change the amounts and the number of line items.

The statement is true.

Cash in vs cash out, not profit vs loss. Planned cash inflows are set against planned cash outflows for a given period to see whether a cash surplus or a shortfall arises. The difference is a cash figure. Bookkeeping determines profit differently. The statement describes exactly this comparison. A cash surplus and a shortfall are the two possible signs of this difference.

The statement is true.

Profit and depreciation do not belong in this comparison. The financial plan sets planned cash inflows against planned cash outflows. Period profit arises in bookkeeping; depreciation is precisely an example of an expense without a cash outflow. Anyone who puts profit and depreciation into the financial plan mixes financial accounting and the income statement. Then a high profit would fake liquidity even though the money is not yet there, or depreciation would fake an outflow that never leaves the account. A planned profit in the P&L says nothing about the next weeks' cash without inflows and outflows.

The statement is false.

Shortfall means need. If planned outflows exceed planned inflows, a shortfall remains, and that means a financing need. The company must then raise funds or postpone outflows. The statement couples the sign of the difference to the financing question that financial accounting is meant to answer.

The statement is true.

Month as an example, not the only grid. The period can be, for example, one month. Weekly slices or longer horizons are not ruled out, but the monthly example shows that the plan should be periodic and concrete, not only an annual fiction. The statement takes over the example correctly.

The statement is true.

title: Cash inflows and cash outflows
context: Assess the following statements on cash inflows, cash outflows, receipts and expenditures:
statements: Most receipts also constitute cash inflows, and most expenditures also constitute cash outflows.
Differences between a receipt and a cash inflow can arise in time when a receipt only later becomes a cash inflow.
A substantive difference exists when an expenditure is not accompanied by a cash outflow, for example in the case of depreciation.
Receipt and cash inflow are regularly identical in financial accounting; timing or substantive differences play practically no role.
In connection with financial accounting, the terms cash inflow and cash outflow are more precise than receipts and expenditures.
tactical_explanations:
Mostly yes, always no. Business logic notes that most receipts are also cash inflows and most expenditures are also cash outflows. That is the basic closeness of the pairs, not their complete identity. That is exactly why the exceptions follow in the next sentence. The statement stays with this majority finding.

The statement is true.

Time shifts the money. A receipt may already exist while the related cash inflow only later lands in the account, for example with a later payment receipt. Then the terms diverge in time. For financial accounting what counts is the payment moment, not the earlier recognition of the receipt. The statement names exactly this timing difference.

The statement is true.

Depreciation burdens the result, not the account. An expenditure can occur without a cash outflow; the example is depreciation. The consumption of value of a fixed asset is recorded as expenditure or expense; no cash flows out in that period. Anyone who treats depreciation like a bank transfer overestimates the liquidity outflow. The statement hits the substantive difference. The machine loses value; the bank balance is untouched by this booking step.

The statement is true.

Differences arise in time or substance — that is why cash inflow/cash outflow are the more precise terms in financial accounting.

The statement is false.

Precision follows from the differences. Because receipts and expenditures do not always coincide with payments, cash inflow and cash outflow are the more apt terms in connection with financial accounting. The financial plan should depict liquidity, not period result. The statement takes over this terminological choice. Due invoices are planned with cash inflows and outflows, not with accounting profit.

The statement is true.

title: Cash surplus and reserves
context: Assess the following statements on the case where cash inflows exceed cash outflows:
statements: If cash inflows exceed cash outflows, solvency is given.
If the surplus is very high, the entire amount may be invested permanently so that it is no longer available in the following months.
In subsequent periods, cash outflows can be higher than cash inflows, so that the surpluses are soon needed again.
Financial reserves that can be accessed quickly are especially important for unforeseen payments that are not included in financial planning.
A cash surplus in one month rules out that a financing need arises again later.
tactical_explanations:
The sign decides liquidity. Cash in minus cash out: if the difference is positive, inflows exceed outflows, and solvency is given. Business logic couples this constellation not to profit but to the cash surplus. Example: inflows €80,000, outflows €65,000, surplus €15,000. The statement holds the rule. If inflows lie below, the sign flips and solvency is no longer given.

The statement is true.

Invest yes, lock away no. With a very high surplus one should consider whether part is better invested than left in the bank account. At the same time: in following weeks or months outflows can be higher; the surpluses are then needed again. Anyone who permanently ties up the entire surplus so it is unavailable in following months ignores exactly this warning. Liquidity this month is no licence for illiquidity next month. Part can be invested, but only so that quickly available funds remain for the next periods.

The statement is false.

Next month can flip. The presentation expressly warns that in following periods outflows can be higher and today's surpluses will soon be needed again. A financial plan is a chain of slices, not a one-off all-clear. The statement restates this timing caution.

The statement is true.

The unforeseen needs a quick buffer. Unforeseen payments often do not appear in the financial plan and can suddenly burden liquidity. That requires financial reserves that can be accessed quickly, not only long-term locked investments. The reserve protects solvency between planned inflows and outflows. Exactly this function is what the statement names.

The statement is true.

One month does not prove the year. A cash surplus shows that in that period inflows exceed outflows. The next period can reverse the sign; business logic expressly reckons with higher later outflows. Financing need can therefore arise again. The absolute claim that a surplus rules out later need contradicts the period logic of financial planning. Financial planning works in slices, each with its own sign of inflows minus outflows.

The statement is false.

title: Measures in case of a shortfall
context: Assess the following statements on the case where cash outflows exceed cash inflows:
statements: If cash outflows exceed cash inflows, solvency is at risk and the company must take countermeasures immediately.
Possible measures include reducing expenditures, agreeing longer payment terms with suppliers, and granting customers only short payment terms.
Reducing inventory levels or taking a short-term bank loan can support solvency.
If insolvency threatens repeatedly and cannot easily be remedied, admitting further shareholders can help.
If outflows exceed inflows, it is enough to wait until liquidity restores itself.
tactical_explanations:
Danger demands action. Outflows over inflows means threatened solvency. Business logic requires immediate countermeasures, not calm observation until the year-end accounts. Every further day with uncovered due invoices brings insolvency closer. The statement correctly couples the sign and the duty to act. If management waits, due invoices stay unpaid and insolvency draws nearer.

The statement is true.

Payment terms are a liquidity lever. Cut expenditures, lengthen supplier terms and shorten customer terms: money should leave later and arrive earlier. These are operational steps that shift inflows and outflows without yet changing the legal form. Together with expenditure cuts they belong to the typical measures for a shortfall. The statement lists them correctly.

The statement is true.

Inventory and credit reach into the cash drawer. Reducing inventory frees tied-up money; a short-term bank loan temporarily fills the gap. Both stand on the measures list. Neither replaces the financial plan nor makes the problem invisible, but both can support immediate solvency.

The statement is true.

Repetition changes the tool. If insolvency keeps recurring and cannot easily be remedied, business logic names capital contributions by new shareholders as a way to improve and secure liquidity permanently. That is equity, not only a short loan. The statement hits this escalation step. That is equity from outside, not just another short-term credit that would already burden the next instalment.

The statement is true.

Waiting is not a countermeasure. The presentation says: solvency is at risk; the company must act immediately. Anyone who waits leaves due invoices unpaid. Insolvency threatens precisely when liquidity is missing. Hope of self-healing contradicts the expressly required intervention. Business logic demands immediate countermeasures: cut expenditures, flip payment terms, reduce inventory or take a loan, if necessary new capital contributions. Waiting is not on that list. Without such steps the difference outflows minus inflows stays uncovered.

The statement is false.

title: Financial plan at start-up
context: Assess the following statements on financial planning by company founders:
statements: In the course of founding, comparatively high cash outflows must already be made, while usually there are still no cash inflows and also no experience values for future cash inflows.
Exactly for that reason founders often have to submit a financial plan with financing applications.
This financial plan should be planned cautiously and realistically so that capital providers can be convinced.
Founders can calculate cash inflows just as securely as established businesses with long payment series.
Financial accounting has great business significance, among other reasons because without solvency insolvency threatens.
tactical_explanations:
Outflows first, inflows later. At founding, comparatively high outflows arise; inflows are usually still missing, and experience values for how much inflow can be calculated are also missing. The financial plan thus stands on uncertain ground and is nonetheless indispensable. The statement describes exactly this imbalance. Exactly for that reason the financial plan at founding is harder than in ongoing operations with known payment series.

The statement is true.

Capital wants to see the plan. Because the founding situation is so uncertain, founders often must submit a financial plan with financing applications. The plan is the instrument with which solvency is argued to capital providers. The statement links application and plan as business logic does.

The statement is true.

Caution instead of window-dressing. The plan should be cautious and realistic so that capital providers can be convinced. Excessively high inflow assumptions destroy credibility and later lead into a liquidity gap. The statement holds the quality standard that the presentation places on the founding financial plan.

The statement is true.

Experience values are precisely what is missing. Business logic stresses that usually there are still no inflows and also no experience values for how much inflow can be calculated. Established businesses can extrapolate series; start-ups cannot to the same degree. Claiming equal certainty erases exactly the founding problem that makes the financial plan so hard and so important. Anyone who claims the same certainty as established businesses erases the reason capital providers demand a cautious plan. The financial plan replaces missing time series with cautious assumptions, not with fake certainty.

The statement is false.

Without cash, no continued existence. Financial accounting has great business significance because solvency must be secured at all times and its absence can lead to insolvency. Founding, ongoing operations and raising capital all depend on it. The statement summarises this significance without replacing bookkeeping. Founding, ongoing operations and financing applications hang on the same question: whether inflows cover due outflows.

The statement is true.

title: Cash flow and solvency
context: Assess the following statements on cash flow in financial accounting:
statements: Cash flow is determined by setting cash inflows and cash outflows within a given period against each other.
If in this period cash inflows exceed cash outflows, cash flow is positive — there is a cash inflow to the company.
A positive cash flow is an indicator of solvency.
That is of great importance among other things for investments and for loan repayments.
A positive cash flow is identical with period profit because both measure the same surplus of the period.
tactical_explanations:
Cash flow is a cash difference. Cash inflows and outflows of a given period are set against each other. That follows the same logic as in the financial plan, now named as a ratio. Profit via revenues and expenses is a different calculation path. Anyone who confuses cash flow with profit mixes the cash and performance levels.

The statement is true.

Plus sign means inflow. Inflows greater than outflows yield a positive cash flow — a cash/money inflow to the company. Example: inflows €120,000, outflows €95,000, cash flow +€25,000. The sign describes the cash movement, not automatically the period result. The statement hits the definition. The sign describes the period's cash movement, not automatically the P&L period result.

The statement is true.

Indicator, not identical with profit. A positive cash flow shows that in the period more money flowed in than out, and therefore counts as an indicator of solvency.
