A later point adds that one can have profit without liquidity and liquidity without profit. As an indicator in financial accounting, positive cash flow nonetheless remains valid.

The statement is true.

Investing and repaying need money. Investments and loan repayments are cash outflows. Without cash inflow or existing liquidity they cannot be made. Business logic highlights the importance of positive cash flow exactly for these two purposes. The statement follows this link.

The statement is true.

Cash flow compares inflows and outflows; profit results from revenues and expenses. The two can diverge.

The statement is false.

title: Bookkeeping as external accounting
context: Assess the following statements on bookkeeping and its circle of addressees:
statements: Every company is legally obliged to determine its profit or loss for each financial year.
That is significant not least for calculating income taxes, which depending on legal form the entrepreneur or the company must pay.
Bookkeeping is also called external accounting because it has an information and documentation function towards the outside.
Only the tax authorities have an interest in the period result; company management, capital providers and employees remain uninvolved.
Company management must decide whether profit is withdrawn or distributed or left in the company, for example to invest in machines or other assets.
tactical_explanations:
Duty, not optional. Every company must determine profit or loss for each financial year. That is a legal obligation, regardless of whether cost accounting already runs internally. The statement restates this duty before EAR or double-entry bookkeeping are distinguished. The choice between EAR and double-entry later changes only the method, not the annual determination duty.

The statement is true.

Tax follows the result. Determination serves not least the calculation of income taxes. Depending on legal form, the person or the company pays. Without period result there is no tax base. The statement holds this tax reason without denying other addressees. Liquidity in financial accounting does not replace this tax calculation base.

The statement is true.

Inform and document outwards. Because bookkeeping serves addressees outside the business, it is also called external accounting. Cost accounting later stands opposite as internal accounting. External effect and naming hang together: balance sheet and P&L address creditors, owners and authorities. The statement hits exactly this outward function.

The statement is true.

Many stakeholders, not only the tax office. Business logic names, besides the tax authority, company management, capital providers, shareholders (for example stockholders), business partners (for example suppliers) and employees. Anyone who allows only the authority erases exactly this list. Management needs the result to judge how successfully the business was run, capital providers for their investment, suppliers for the creditworthiness of the relationship.

The statement is false.

Distribute or retain is a management decision. After profit comes the use question: withdrawal or distribution, or retention in the company, for example for machines and other assets. Retention strengthens internal financing and equity. Management weighs liquidity need and investment goals. The statement describes exactly this choice.

The statement is true.

title: EAR and double-entry bookkeeping
context: Assess the following statements on the receipts-and-payments account (EAR) and double-entry bookkeeping:
statements: In the receipts-and-payments account, the receipts of a financial year are set against expenditures; the expenditures essentially correspond to cash outflows but also include depreciation.

Under double-entry bookkeeping, a balance sheet and a profit and loss statement are prepared; profit is determined in the P&L and must also result from comparing equity at the beginning and at the end of the financial year.
Sole proprietorships and partnerships whose turnover is under €700,000 per financial year can prepare an EAR.
If they exceed this turnover threshold or if a corporation is involved, double-entry bookkeeping must be kept.
The receipts-and-payments account determines the period result primarily by setting assets against liabilities at a reporting date.
tactical_explanations:
EAR mixes payments and depreciation. Receipts of a financial year stand against expenditures. Expenditures essentially correspond to cash outflows but also include depreciation. Thus EAR is closer to cash than the P&L, but not purely cash-based. The statement restates exactly this construction. EAR is closer to cash than the P&L, but not purely cash-based, because depreciation is still included.

The statement is true.

Double because two paths show the same profit. Balance sheet and P&L are prepared. Profit stands in the P&L and at the same time as the change in equity between the beginning and end of the financial year. Both must yield the same amount — hence double profit determination and the name double-entry bookkeeping. The statement holds both paths. If the two paths diverge, double determination is not fulfilled.

The statement is true.

Threshold €700,000 turnover. Sole proprietorships and partnerships under this threshold per financial year may choose the less elaborate EAR. That is a may-rule, not a compulsion to use EAR. Corporations are not yet in this group. The statement hits the threshold and the circle of addressees.

The statement is true.

Threshold or legal form flips the system. If entrepreneurs exceed the €700,000 turnover threshold or if a corporation is involved, double-entry bookkeeping must be kept. A GmbH therefore falls under the duty regardless of whether someone would find EAR more convenient. Both triggers stand alternatively side by side. The statement links them correctly.

The statement is true.

Setting assets against liabilities is balance-sheet logic. EAR sets receipts and expenditures of a financial year against each other.

The statement is false.

title: Assets, equity and liabilities, and the balance-sheet equation
context: Assess the following statements on the structure of the balance sheet:
statements: The assets side shows the assets — for example land, buildings, machines and inventories.
The equity-and-liabilities side shows how these assets have been financed — with own funds or with external funds.
Assets equal capital applies — that is, the sum of assets equals the sum of equity and liabilities — because every part of the assets must have been financed.
Assets stand on the debit side of the balance sheet; equity and liabilities stand on the credit side.
Equity and liabilities stand on the debit side because they show what funds have been used for.
tactical_explanations:
Assets are the company's wealth. Land, buildings, machines, inventories and similar items stand on the assets side. They answer what assets the company has. Financing belongs on the other side — the equity-and-liabilities side, not in the asset list.

The statement is true.

Equity and liabilities explain the origin. Own funds are equity; external funds are debt capital. Together they show how the assets on the assets side were financed. Without this side the assets side would remain uncovered. The financing question of the balance sheet is exactly: to whom does the capital that carries the assets belong? Thus the equity-and-liabilities side answers the origin question of the balance sheet.

The statement is true.

Equality is mandatory. Assets equal capital; sum of assets equals sum of equity and liabilities, because every asset item must be financed. An asset position without an equity-or-liability counterpart would not exist in this logic. Total assets and total capital are also called balance-sheet total. The statement restates the identity. An asset without an equity/liability counterpart would not exist; that is why total assets and total capital are also called balance-sheet total.

The statement is true.

Debit left, credit right. Assets stand on the debit side of the balance sheet; equity and liabilities on the credit side; both sides must be equal in height. The difference between assets and debt capital is equity. Anyone who swaps the sides destroys the balance-sheet equation. Placement follows classic account logic. Swapped sides would destroy debit–credit equality.

The statement is true.

Debit is use; credit is origin. In bookkeeping the debit side generally shows what funds have been used for — that is why all assets stand there. The credit side shows where the funds come from — that is why capital stands there. Putting equity and liabilities on the debit side reverses use and origin of funds. The same logic applies to individual transactions: debit use, credit origin. Anyone who puts equity and liabilities on the left twists origin and use.

The statement is false.

title: Equity and period result
context: Assess the following statements on equity, debt capital and comparing two balance sheets:
statements: If assets exceed debt capital, the positive difference is equity — that part of the assets that has not been financed with debt.
If one compares the balance sheets of two points in time, a rise in equity means a profit.
A fall in equity between two points in time means a loss.
The comparison in the balance sheet is made at a specific point in time, usually at the end of a financial year.
A rise in debt capital between two reporting dates already counts in itself as a profit.
tactical_explanations:
Equity is a residual. Assets minus debt capital — that is, liabilities — yields the positive difference equity: the part of the assets not financed with debt. If more assets than liabilities stand there, the company is in that sense richer in own funds. The statement restates exactly this difference.

The statement is true.

Two reporting dates, one performance message. If equity rises from one balance-sheet date to the next, that means a profit. That is the same profit the P&L shows, only via the capital comparison. Withdrawals can overlay the picture; the presentation nonetheless links the rise to profit. The statement follows this rule.

The statement is true.

Falling equity means loss. If equity falls between two points in time, the company has become poorer. The P&L and the equity comparison must carry the same loss message. A rise would be profit; a fall is the loss side. The statement holds exactly this period logic.

The statement is true.

The balance sheet is a reporting-date photo. Assets and capital are set against each other at a specific point in time, usually at the end of a financial year. P&L and financial plan work over periods; the balance sheet photographs the reporting date. Anyone who reads the balance sheet as a period calculation mixes three instruments. The statement hits the time logic.

The statement is true.

More debt is not profit. Profit is the rise in equity or the surplus of revenues over expenses. Debt capital is liabilities. If the company takes additional loans, debt capital rises and often assets too, without that already being a profit. Anyone who equates a rise in debt capital with profit confuses origin of funds with period result. Means of financing are not period result.

The statement is false.

title: FunBike: assets and current-asset intensity
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (amounts in euro) shows on the assets side land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000 and bank balances and cash 320,250. The equity-and-liabilities side comprises cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000 and trade payables 300,000. Total assets and total capital each amount to 9,638,250. Assess the following statements on this balance sheet:
statements: Total assets and total capital are called the balance-sheet total and here each amount to €9,638,250.
FunBike GmbH's non-current assets exceed four million euro.
Current assets amount to €6,318,250, and within them inventories dominate at €5,400,000.
The company is current-asset intensive because it has clearly more current assets than non-current assets.
Bank balances and cash exceed inventories.
tactical_explanations:
Both sides the same total. Total assets or total capital are called the balance-sheet total. Adding the assets: 750,000 + 2,330,000 + 240,000 + 5,400,000 + 598,000 + 320,250 = 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities: 525,000 + 3,614,250 + 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 + 300,000 = 9,638,250. The identity assets equal capital holds. The statement hits the label and the amount. The identity holds because every asset position must be financed.

The statement is true.

Non-current assets stay under four million. Non-current assets are assets meant to remain longer than one year: land and buildings 750,000 plus technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000 plus financial assets 240,000. 750,000 + 2,330,000 = 3,080,000, plus 240,000 = €3,320,000. Four million would be 4,000,000. 3,320,000 lies below. Business logic later speaks of somewhat more than three million euro of long-term assets, matching this sum. The claim that non-current assets exceed four million is therefore false.

The statement is false.

Current assets calculation. Inventories 5,400,000 plus receivables 598,000 plus bank balances and cash 320,250. 5,400,000 + 598,000 = 5,998,000, plus 320,250 = €6,318,250. Inventories alone are 5,400,000 and thus the clearly largest block. Business logic calls that plausible for a bicycle producer. The statement hits the total and the dominance.

The statement is true.

Current assets lie clearly above non-current assets. FunBike shows €6,318,250 current assets against €3,320,000 non-current assets. The company is therefore current-asset intensive: short-term tied values dominate. Inventories especially drive this structure. The classification follows the size comparison of the two asset blocks.

The statement is true.

Cash against warehouse: the warehouse wins. Bank balances and cash stand at €320,250, inventories at €5,400,000. 320,250 is far smaller, not larger. The claim reverses the relationship. Precisely because inventories weigh so heavily, the question of inventory reduction arises. The statement is numerically false. Inventories clearly dominate the assets side versus cash.

The statement is false.

title: FunBike: capital structure and golden balance-sheet rule
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (amounts in euro) shows cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000 and trade payables 300,000. The balance-sheet total is €9,638,250; non-current assets are €3,320,000. Assess the following statements on financing:
statements: Equity amounts to €4,139,250.
Around 57 percent of capital is debt capital, the bulk of it bank loans.
Such a capital structure with high dependence on debt capital is not atypical for Austrian small and medium-sized enterprises.

The golden balance-sheet rule is met because the long-term tied assets of somewhat more than three million euro are covered by equity of over four million euro and presumably also by long-term debt capital.
Equity lies under three million euro and is therefore not enough to finance non-current assets on a long-term basis.
tactical_explanations:
Add equity. Cash contributions 525,000 plus profit 3,614,250. 525,000 + 3,614,250 = €4,139,250. That is the part of equity and liabilities that is not debt capital. Check: debt capital 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 + 300,000 = 5,499,000, plus 4,139,250 = 9,638,250, the balance-sheet total. The statement hits the amount.

The statement is true.

Debt-capital ratio. Debt capital 5,499,000 divided by balance-sheet total 9,638,250. 5,499,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.5705, so around 57 percent. Of that, bank loans 3,199,000, the largest debt block before provisions 2,000,000 and payables 300,000. Business logic names exactly these around 57 percent and bank loans as the bulk. The statement matches the calculation. 3,199,000 of 5,499,000 confirms that bank loans carry the bulk of debt capital, ahead of provisions and trade payables.

The statement is true.

SME pattern, not a scandal. The presentation places FunBike with a balance-sheet total just under €10 million still among small enterprises and holds high debt dependence typical for Austrian SMEs. The observed structure is therefore expected, not a special case. The high profit does, however, strengthen equity and internal financing if it remains in the company.

The statement is true.

Long-term covered by long-term. The golden balance-sheet rule requires that long-term tied assets should be financed long-term. Non-current assets 3,320,000 — somewhat more than three million. Equity 4,139,250, so over four million, and part of debt capital will presumably be long-term. 4,139,250 already covers 3,320,000 alone. The rule is met. The statement restates this check. Were equity smaller than long-term assets and long-term debt missing, the rule would be breached.

The statement is true.

Four million, not under three. Equity 4,139,250 lies over four million, not under three. Non-current assets 3,320,000 are smaller than this equity. The claim understates equity and wrongly explains that it does not suffice for long-term financing. Exactly the opposite supports the golden balance-sheet rule.

The statement is false.

title: Profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH
context: In the P&L, expenses are deducted from sales revenues and other income. The profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx shows sales revenues €70,656,000, material expense €53,175,000, personnel expense €7,900,000, depreciation €1,800,000, other operating expenses €2,875,000, interest income €12,000, interest expense €99,000, taxes €1,204,750 and annual result €3,614,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: If the sum of revenues and income exceeds expenses, a profit is achieved.
Expenses in the P&L include among other things wages and salaries, material expense, rent, insurance expense, energy expense, depreciation of tangible assets and the creation of provisions.
FunBike GmbH's annual result amounts to €3,614,250 and corresponds to the profit reported in the balance sheet.
Depreciation of €1,800,000 increases profit in the P&L because it is not a cash outflow.
The same profit can also be determined by comparing equity at the beginning and at the end of the financial year; both must agree, which is why one speaks of double profit determination.
tactical_explanations:
Income over expense is profit. In the P&L, expenses are deducted from sales revenues and other income. If a positive remainder stays, the company has become richer in the period. Conversely a loss arises. The statement restates this sign rule, still without the FunBike figures.

The statement is true.

Expense list. Wages and salaries, material, rent, insurance, energy, depreciation of tangible assets such as machines, creation of provisions: business logic counts all of that among expenses. FunBike shows material, personnel, depreciation and other operating expenses as concrete blocks. The statement stays with the concept list, not a single line item.

The statement is true.

Calculate from top to bottom. Sales revenues 70,656,000 minus material 53,175,000 = 17,481,000. Minus personnel 7,900,000 = 9,581,000. Minus depreciation 1,800,000 = 7,781,000. Minus other operating expenses 2,875,000 = 4,906,000, the EBIT. Interest income 12,000 minus interest expense 99,000 = financial result −87,000. 4,906,000 − 87,000 = 4,819,000 before tax. Minus taxes 1,204,750 = 3,614,250 annual result. The same amount stands in the balance sheet as profit. The statement hits the figure and the bridge to the balance sheet.

The statement is true.

Depreciation reduces; it does not increase. After deducting material and personnel, €9,581,000 remain. Depreciation of €1,800,000 is an expense and is deducted: 9,581,000 minus 1,800,000 = 7,781,000. Without this deduction the intermediate result would be €1,800,000 higher, and later profit likewise. That depreciation is not a cash outflow belongs in financial accounting and in distinguishing cash flow from profit. In the P&L it remains an expense with a minus sign. The claim that it increases profit reverses this sign.

The statement is false.

Two paths, one figure. Profit increases equity and can also be determined by comparing current equity with that at the beginning of the financial year. P&L and equity comparison must show the same profit — hence double profit determination and in this context double-entry bookkeeping. FunBike reports 3,614,250 in both roles, as annual result and as profit in the balance sheet. The statement hits the system.

The statement is true.

title: Cash-flow statement and profit
context: Assess the following statements on the cash-flow statement and its relationship to profit:
statements: Cash flow is not identical with profit, because one can achieve a profit without having liquid funds, and one can be liquid without achieving a profit.
In the cash-flow statement the operating activities area is the most important, because it concerns the core of the business and shows whether cash surpluses are earned there.
A positive cash flow is identical with accounting profit because both measure the same surplus.
In the investing area, cash flows into the acquisition of non-current assets, while the sale of non-current assets can generate cash.
Cash flow and profit are the same ratio because every depreciation is at the same time a cash outflow and every sale is at the same time a cash inflow.
tactical_explanations:
Two truths side by side. Published annual financial statements contain, besides balance sheet and P&L, a cash-flow statement or statement of cash flows. Cash flow measures solvency; profit measures period result. One can have profit without liquid funds — for example with high receivables and depreciation — and be liquid without profit, for example after taking a loan. The statement holds exactly this non-identity.

The statement is true.

Operations first. The operating activities area concerns the core of the business. Investors often look especially here because it shows whether the core earns cash surpluses. Financing and investing explain other causes of inflows and outflows. The statement hits this ranking.

The statement is true.

Cash flow and profit can diverge; liquidity and period result are not the same.

The statement is false.

Investing is buying and selling assets. If money flows into acquiring long-term investments, for example non-current assets, that is an outflow in the investing area. Selling land or a building can conversely generate cash there. That is not operating activity and not mere borrowing. The statement restates both directions.

The statement is true.

Depreciation separates the two figures. In financial accounting, depreciation is the example of an expenditure without a cash outflow. In the P&L it reduces profit; no money leaves the account in that step. Sales revenues can already be income as receivables before the cash inflow comes. Therefore cash flow and profit are not the same ratio. The claim that every depreciation is a cash outflow and every sale a cash inflow erases exactly the differences for which business logic places both statements side by side.

The statement is false.

title: Purpose of cost accounting
context: Assess the following statements on cost accounting:
statements: Cost accounting should show how much a manufactured product or a provided service costs.
A company can exist permanently even if costs are permanently not covered by revenues.
Every company must legally keep cost accounting.
Cost accounting counts as internal accounting because it is used only internally.
Small companies keep cost accounting especially often and reliably.
tactical_explanations:
Unit costs are the entry into control. Cost accounting has two questions: how much does the product manufactured or the service provided in the company cost, and how much does the revenue from the sale contribute to covering costs. Without this calculation it remains unclear whether a bicycle or a service justifies the consumption of machines, labour and input materials. Exactly for that reason a company must know its costs, not only the profit from bookkeeping. The task is internal and business-related, not merely a compulsory exercise for the company register. Anyone who only knows annual profit still does not know whether the individual bike covers its costs. Cost accounting supplements bookkeeping exactly with this unit and service view.

The statement is true.

Without coverage by revenues no business lasts permanently. In the long run no company can exist if costs are not covered by revenues. A single loss year may be bridgeable; permanent under-coverage eats substance and solvency. The statement claims the opposite and erases the existence condition that cost-accounting theory places first. Anyone who ignores costs because somewhere turnover is still visible confuses movement with cost coverage.

The statement is false.

No law forces cost accounting. It is not legally mandatory, unlike profit determination in bookkeeping. Business-wise it is advantageous as a steering and control instrument, but that does not make it a duty. Anyone who derives a legal duty from the benefit mixes internal and external accounting. Small businesses often omit it even though it would be useful — exactly that shows there is no compulsion.

The statement is false.

Internal means: the figures stay in-house. Cost accounting is called internal accounting because it is used only internally. It serves management as a steering and control instrument, not publication towards the tax authority or company register. Capital providers see the annual financial statements, not necessarily the unit costing. Exactly this demarcation from bookkeeping's external accounting is what the sentence carries.

The statement is true.

Small businesses often do not keep it. It is noted that cost accounting especially in small companies frequently does not take place, even though it would be business-advantageous. The claim that it is kept there especially often and reliably reverses this observation. Size and duty diverge here: missing legal obligation and scarce capacity explain the gap, not particular care.

The statement is false.

title: Internal and external accounting
context: A bicycle manufactory in Graz keeps bookkeeping and cost accounting. Assess the following statements:
statements: Bookkeeping is called external accounting because it has an information and documentation function towards the outside.
Capital providers, shareholders and suppliers have an interest in the profit or loss of the financial year.
Cost accounting must use the same statutory structure as the balance sheet and the profit and loss statement.
As a steering and control instrument, cost accounting is business-advantageous.
Owners receive cost accounting by law in the same form as the published annual financial statements.
tactical_explanations:
Outwards, bookkeeping documents, not costing. Every company must determine profit or loss for the financial year, not least because of income taxes. That is why bookkeeping is called external accounting: it informs and documents towards the tax authority, capital providers, shareholders, business partners and employees. The Graz manufactory thus accounts for assets and performance, regardless of how detailed internal costing is.

The statement is true.

Many stakeholder groups read the same result. Whether profit or loss was achieved interests not only the tax authority but also company management, capital providers, shareholders such as stockholders, business partners such as suppliers, and employees. The annual financial statements answer whether the company became richer or poorer in the period. Exactly this interest grounds the documentation function outwards. Cost accounting does not replace this view; it supplements it internally. Without this external report, capital providers and the tax authority would lack a common figures base. Internal unit costings do not replace this documentation duty and may be cut differently.

The statement is true.

No statutory corset for the internal account. Cost accounting is not legally mandatory and is used only internally. It therefore need not have the same structure as balance sheet and P&L. Management can structure fixed costs, variable costs and contribution margins as decisions require. Anyone who internally demands the same compulsory structure as for the annual financial statements transfers rules of external accounting to an instrument that theory expressly calls internal and voluntary.

The statement is false.

Steering and controlling need costs, not only annual profit. Business-wise it is advantageous to keep cost accounting as a steering and control instrument. Unit costs, additional orders and break-even cannot be read from the P&L alone. The manufactory decides on prices and accepting orders with these internal figures. The statement hits exactly this benefit without claiming a legal duty.

The statement is true.

Ownership does not make costing a compulsory publication. Owners and shareholders count among the stakeholders of bookkeeping; published annual financial statements comprise balance sheet, P&L and often a cash-flow statement. Cost accounting remains internal and is not legally mandatory. A legal equation with the published annual financial statements is not invented by the theory. Internal reports can be more frequent and cut differently; they do not replace the external statements.

The statement is false.

title: Costs and expenses
context: Assess the following statements on the relationship between costs and expenses:
statements: Costs in most cases largely correspond to the expenses in bookkeeping.
Additional costs not recognised in bookkeeping are possible, for example the entrepreneur's salary.
The entrepreneur's salary of a sole proprietor stands as an expense in bookkeeping just as firmly as wages of employed staff.
The entrepreneur's salary can be oriented to opportunity costs — that is, to income achievable elsewhere.
Costs are the same as cash outflows in financial accounting.
tactical_explanations:
Largely the same, not word-for-word in every item. Costs in most cases largely correspond to the expenses in bookkeeping. Wages, material, rent and energy appear in both accounting circles. Differences nonetheless remain possible. The statement describes the closeness without claiming identity. Anyone who thinks costs and expenses are completely separate worlds overdoes the distinction; anyone who holds them forever identical suppresses the next point of the definition. Material, wages and energy therefore often appear in both circles, while the entrepreneur's salary makes the gap visible.

The statement is true.

Additional costs sit beside bookkeeping. Additional costs not recognised in bookkeeping are possible — for example the entrepreneur's salary for sole proprietors or OG partners and general partners. That is the remuneration they expect for their work. Internally it belongs in cost accounting so that the performance does not appear free of charge. Exactly this gap between internal consumption and external expense is named.

The statement is true.

The entrepreneur's salary is often a calculated figure of cost accounting and does not automatically stand as an expense in bookkeeping.

The statement is false.

Being able to earn elsewhere sets the measuring stick. The entrepreneur's salary can be oriented to opportunity costs — that is, to the income the entrepreneurs could earn if they pursued another occupational activity. Internally it then becomes visible whether self-employed work at least covers the forgone salary. That is not a cash outflow to third parties but a valuation yardstick. The statement hits exactly this orientation.

The statement is true.

Consumption is not the same as cash outflow. Costs are the valued consumption of performance factors in production or service provision. Cash outflows belong to financial accounting and concern liquidity. Depreciation is expense and often costs without being a cash outflow in the period; the entrepreneur's salary can be costs without bookkeeping expense. Anyone who equates costs with cash outflows mixes cost accounting and financial accounting.

The statement is false.

title: The concept of costs
context: Assess the following statements on what costs are:
statements: Costs are the valued consumption of performance factors in production or service provision.
Performance factors include, for example, machines, labour and input materials.
Between costs and expenses there are usually no differences.
Fixed costs arise independently of the quantity produced or provided.
Variable costs generally fall when the production quantity rises.
tactical_explanations:
Consumption with a value approach, not mere piece-counting. Costs are the valued consumption of performance factors in a company's production or service provision. Machine hours, labour and input materials are valued in money once they enter the performance. Without this concept it remains unclear what cost accounting even measures. The statement restates the definition, not a colloquial equation with invoices from suppliers. Without a money value only a technical quantity list would remain, which cannot be settled with prices and contribution margins. Exactly this valuation turns consumption into a cost figure of cost accounting.

The statement is true.

Three examples make consumption tangible. Performance factors are, for example, machines, labour and input materials. A bicycle works consumes frames and gear parts, working time on the line and wear of assembly plant. All three belong in costs once they enter the performance in value terms. The statement lists exactly the definition's examples without artificially narrowing the circle to material alone.

The statement is true.

Some differences deliberately remain. Costs largely correspond to expenses, but there are some differences — for example the entrepreneur's salary. The claim that there are never differences erases exactly this reservation. Internally a consumption can be calculated that bookkeeping does not show as expense. Anyone who forces identity makes the distinction of the two accounting circles superfluous.

The statement is false.

Quantity changes nothing about fixed costs as long as capacity holds. Fixed costs arise independently of the quantity produced or provided. Management salaries, site rent and insurance continue whether 10 or 10,000 bikes are assembled. The distinction presupposes knowing which costs change when quantity rises and which do not. The statement hits the definition of fixed costs.

The statement is true.

They rise with quantity; they do not fall. Variable costs generally rise proportionally to the quantity produced. For bicycles that is essentially the cost of the components. Anyone who claims variable costs fall with rising quantity reverses the direction. Unit costs can fall through fixed-cost degression; the variable costs of the additional bikes nonetheless rise with quantity.

The statement is false.

title: Fixed and variable costs
context: A business manufactures bicycles. Assess the following statements on fixed and variable costs:
statements: Salaries for management count among fixed costs.
Rent for the production site counts among fixed costs if rent is payable.
The costs of the components from which the bikes are assembled are essentially variable costs.
Depreciation is variable costs and rises proportionally to the quantity produced.
When deciding on an additional order one looks at which additional costs arise through that order.
tactical_explanations:
Management is not newly hired per bike. Fixed costs arise independently of how many bikes are produced in a period. They include salaries for management. Whether assembly runs quieter or fuller typically does not change these salaries in the period considered. The statement correctly assigns the item to fixed costs, as in the bicycle example of the definition.

The statement is true.

Space costs even with an empty hall. Rent for the production site counts among fixed costs if rent is payable. It does not hang on the number of bikes but on the contract for the space. Insurance stands in the same group. Anyone who treats rent as a proportional material item confuses site costs with components.

The statement is true.

Every additional bike needs parts. Variable costs generally rise proportionally to the quantity produced. For bicycles that is essentially the cost of the components from which the bikes are assembled. Frames, tyres and gears follow the unit count. Exactly for that reason they must at least be covered in the price before one can speak of a contribution margin.

The statement is true.

Depreciation is at least partly fixed costs and does not rise proportionally to quantity.

The statement is false.

Additional order means: which costs newly arise. When deciding whether to accept or reject an additional order, one looks at which additional costs arise through that order. Already existing fixed costs of the hall and management often do not change with the individual order. What matters are the additionally consumed components and further attributable extra costs. Exactly this view separates the theory from the question of full unit costs of a normal programme. Ongoing rent and management salaries are typically unchanged by the individual additional order. That is why the question of additionally arising costs is the apt decision figure, not full average unit costs including all fixed costs.

The statement is true.

title: Contribution margin and price
context: Assess the following statements on price, variable costs and contribution margin:
statements: Variable costs should in any case be covered by the price achieved.
If the price exceeds variable costs, a contribution to covering fixed costs arises.
This contribution to covering fixed costs is called the contribution margin.
The contribution margin results from deducting the company's entire fixed costs from the price.
Overall the price should cover total costs — that is, variable and fixed costs.
tactical_explanations:
Below variable costs one sells a loss per unit in the narrow sense. Variable costs should in any case be covered by the price achieved. Without this coverage every additional unit loses extra money before fixed costs even come into play. Components and other quantity-dependent consumption must at least return in the price. The statement sets the lower bound that the theory names before the contribution margin.

The statement is true.

What lies above variable costs works on rent and salaries. If the price achieved exceeds variable costs, a contribution to covering fixed costs is made. Fixed costs arise independently of quantity; without such contributions they remain uncovered. The statement describes exactly this surplus, still without stating the formula unit price minus variable unit costs.

The statement is true.

The name bundles the same surplus. For the contribution to covering fixed costs one speaks of contribution margin. It is the bridge between price and the fixed-cost block, not profit after all costs. Only when the sum of contribution margins exceeds fixed costs does profit arise. The statement places the term correctly at this point.

The statement is true.

The whole business's fixed costs do not belong in the unit formula. A bike's contribution margin is the price minus that bike's variable costs — in the numerical example 400 minus 180 equals €220. One does not deduct millions of total fixed costs from the individual price, or a senselessly negative amount would arise. Fixed costs are settled via the sum of contribution margins or via break-even sales and the contribution ratio. The statement confuses unit calculation and the overall block.

The statement is false.

Long-term, full coverage counts. Overall the price should cover total costs — both variable and fixed costs. The contribution margin is the first hurdle; full cost coverage is the existence condition. Short-term exceptions for unsaleable pre-season goods do not change this target figure.

The statement is true.

title: Short-term price reduction
context: A dealer has bicycles from the previous season that can no longer be sold regularly. Assess the following statements:
statements: A lower price can make sense in the short term if the reduced price exceeds variable costs.
It is more sensible not to sell such a bike at all than to dispose of it more cheaply with a positive contribution margin.
Fixed costs arise in this situation anyway.
In the short term any price below variable costs is business-wise just as sensible as a price above them.
Even with a discount the contribution margin remains a contribution to covering fixed costs.
tactical_explanations:
Unsaleable pre-season goods change the price logic for the moment. In the short term a lower price can make sense if bikes from the previous season can no longer be sold regularly. If the reduced price exceeds variable costs, at least a contribution margin arises. Then something still flows against fixed costs instead of the bike staying put. The statement ties the exception exactly to this condition, not to arbitrary giving away. Regularly the price should still cover variable and fixed costs together. The exception applies only to goods that can no longer be sold at the old price, and only as long as the new price stays above variable costs.

The statement is true.

Leaving it standing is dearer if a contribution is still possible. If the reduced price exceeds variable costs, selling is more sensible than not selling the bike at all. Fixed costs continue; the unsold bike covers nothing. The claim reverses the definition's recommendation. Only if the discount price falls below variable costs would every sale worsen the situation.

The statement is false.

Hall, insurance and management do not wait for the last bike. The contribution margin is a contribution to covering fixed costs that arise anyway. Rent and similar items do not disappear because a previous-season model seems unsaleable. Exactly for that reason a price above variable costs pays: it reduces the uncovered burden without creating new fixed costs.

The statement is true.

Below variable costs even the first contribution is missing. Variable costs should in any case be covered by the price. A price below enlarges the loss per unit and is not just as sensible as a price above. The short-term exception applies only if the reduced price exceeds variable costs. The statement erases this boundary and turns the exception into a licence for any dumping price.

The statement is false.

The name does not change through the discount. Even at the cheaper price one speaks of contribution margin once the price exceeds variable costs: a contribution to covering fixed costs. It turns out smaller than at the regular price but remains the same figure. Profit after full costs need not follow from it. The statement hits the definition that the theory repeats at exactly this point.

The statement is true.

title: Contribution margin €400
context: A company sells a bicycle for €400. Variable costs are €180. Assess the following statements:
statements: The contribution margin is €220 per bike.
The contribution ratio is 55 percent of the selling price.
The contribution margin is €180 per bike.
The contribution ratio results as €180 divided by €400.
55 percent of the selling price can be used to cover fixed costs.
tactical_explanations:
Price minus variable costs, not minus a profit target. €400 selling price minus €180 variable costs yield €220. Exactly this amount is named as the contribution margin for the bike. The €220 stand ready to cover fixed costs before profit arises. Anyone who reads €180 as contribution margin has confused variable costs with the contribution. The identity is: contribution margin = price − variable unit costs = 400 − 180 = 220. €220 is the amount that remains after covering the €180 of components and other quantity costs for rent, insurance and similar fixed costs. Only when such contributions in total exceed fixed costs does profit arise — not already at each individual positive contribution margin.

The statement is true.

Share of the price, not share of the parts. €220 of €400 are 220 / 400 = 0.55, so 55 percent. This percentage is called the contribution ratio. It says which part of each euro of sales can flow to fixed costs once variable costs are earned. The ratio hangs on the relation of contribution to price, not on the mere material value of €180.

The statement is true.

€180 are the variable costs, not the contribution. The contribution margin is 400 minus 180 equals €220. Anyone who states €180 as contribution margin equates the quantity-cost block with the surplus. Then the ratio would be 180 / 400 = 45 percent, which contradicts the theory. The €180 must first be covered; the contribution comes afterwards.

The statement is false.

The ratio hangs on the contribution, not on variable costs alone. Contribution ratio = contribution margin / selling price = 220 / 400 = 55 percent. 180 divided by 400 yields 45 percent and measures the share of variable costs in the price, not the contribution ratio. As a yardstick, 55 percent is expressly with 220 of 400. The wrong division swaps the numerator.

The statement is false.

The same 55-percent logic later carries the break-even. 55 percent of selling prices can be used to cover fixed costs because that is exactly the contribution ratio. Of every sales euro, 55 cents remain after variable costs for the fixed-cost block. With a uniform ratio across all models the same relationship holds for total sales. The statement repeats the bridge the theory strikes from the unit example to the break-even calculation.

The statement is true.

title: Break-even sales
context: Fixed costs are €4 million; the contribution ratio across all bicycle models is 55 percent. Assess the following statements:
statements: Break-even sales amount to 4 million divided by 55 and multiplied by 100 — that is, €7,272,727.27.
The company should achieve at least just under €7.3 million in sales to cover all costs.
Break-even sales result from multiplying €4 million fixed costs by the contribution ratio 0.55.
At sales higher than break-even sales the company enters the profit zone.
By reaching cost coverage at the break-even point the company secures its existence.
tactical_explanations:
Fixed costs equal 55 percent of the sales sought. Fixed costs of €4 million are set equal to the contribution ratio of 55 percent. Then: 4,000,000 / 55 × 100 = €7,272,727.27. Written differently: sales = fixed costs / 0.55 = 4,000,000 / 0.55 = 7,272,727.27. At this sales level the cumulative contribution margins just cover the fixed-cost block. The theory calculates the same path.

The statement is true.

Just under €7.3 million is the rounded threshold. €7,272,727.27 are just under €7.3 million. Below this mark fixed costs remain uncovered; above it the profit zone begins. The statement takes over the qualitative conclusion of the numerical example without inventing a new formula. Securing existence here hangs on full cost coverage through sales, not on an arbitrary sales target.

The statement is true.

Correct is dividing: fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio (or ×100/55), not multiplying.

The statement is false.

Above the threshold contribution remains. At sales higher than break-even the company enters the profit zone. Every further euro of sales delivers, under the assumptions, 55 cents beyond the already covered fixed costs. Below the threshold fixed costs remain partly uncovered. The statement follows directly on the €7.27 million calculation in the theory.

The statement is true.

Cost coverage is the existence condition here. The company should achieve at least just under €7.3 million sales to cover at least all costs; at higher sales it enters the profit zone and thereby secures its existence. In the long run no company can exist if costs are not covered by revenues. The break-even point is exactly this threshold in the numerical example, not a tax compulsory figure.

The statement is true.

title: Structure of the profit and loss statement
context: Assess the following statements on the profit and loss statement:
statements: In the P&L, expenses are deducted from sales revenues and other income.
Expenses include among other things wages and salaries, material expense, rent, insurance, energy, depreciation and the creation of provisions.
If the sum of revenues and income exceeds expenses, a profit is achieved.
Profit in the P&L is to be equated with cash flow in the same period.
Profit increases equity.
tactical_explanations:
Income minus expense — that is the P&L. Expenses are deducted from sales revenues and other income. That produces the period result, not by setting cash inflows against cash outflows. The FunBike figures begin with sales revenues and deduct material, personnel, depreciation and other operating expenses down to EBIT and on to the annual result. The statement describes exactly this structure. Cash inflows and outflows belong in financial and cash-flow accounting. Depreciation and provisions show expense in the P&L that need not be cash in the same period — exactly why the income statement stands beside the cash statement.

The statement is true.

The expense list is broader than material alone. Wages and salaries, material expense, rent, insurance expense, energy expense, depreciation of tangible assets and the creation of provisions count among expenses. Depreciation and provisions show that expense need not be the same as a cash outflow of the period. The statement gathers the definition's examples and marks the P&L as an income statement.

The statement is true.

More income than expense means profit. If the sum of revenues and income exceeds expenses, a profit is achieved. Then the company has become richer in the period in the sense of the bookkeeping question. If expenses lie higher, a loss arises. The statement holds the sign rule without mixing cash flow or unit costs.

The statement is true.

Performance and cash flow diverge. Cash flow is not identical with profit: one can achieve a profit without having liquid funds, and be liquid without achieving a profit. Depreciation reduces profit without cash flowing out in the period; inventory build-up can tie up cash while the P&L still shows profit. The claim of constant identity contradicts exactly this distinction.

The statement is false.

Profit strengthens equity on the equity-and-liabilities side. Profit increases equity and can also be determined by comparing current equity with that at the beginning of the financial year. In the FunBike balance sheet the profit of €3,614,250 stands expressly in equity. Withdrawal or distribution would be the opposite movement. The statement hits the effect that the theory attributes to the P&L and double profit determination.

The statement is true.

title: Double profit determination
context: Assess the following statements on double profit determination:
statements: Profit is determined in the profit and loss statement.
Profit can also be determined by comparing equity at the beginning and at the end of a financial year.
Both paths must yield the same profit.
This double profit determination is connected with the term double-entry bookkeeping.
The receipts-and-payments account counts as double-entry bookkeeping because it includes depreciation.
tactical_explanations:
The P&L is the first path to the period result. Under double-entry bookkeeping, balance sheet and profit and loss statement arise; profit is determined in the P&L. Sales revenues and income minus expenses lead to the annual result. FunBike shows this path to €3,614,250. The statement names one of the two prescribed paths without excluding the equity comparison. The same amount must reappear in the equity comparison, or double determination would be broken.

The statement is true.

Rising equity tells the same story. Profit can also be determined by comparing equity at the beginning and at the end of a financial year. If equity rises, there is profit; if it falls, loss — provided withdrawals and contributions are properly accounted for. The balance sheets of two reporting dates thus deliver the second measurement. Both paths stand side by side. Withdrawals and contributions must be properly separated, or a private withdrawal would look like a loss.

The statement is true.

Same profit, or the bookkeeping does not add up. Both determinations must yield the same profit — hence double profit determination. If P&L and equity comparison diverge, there is an error in the transactions or in the closing work. Agreement is the control, not a rough approximation. The statement restates exactly this must-condition.

The statement is true.

The name double-entry bookkeeping hangs on this doubling. One speaks of double profit determination and in this connection also of double-entry bookkeeping: balance sheet plus P&L, profit on two paths. That is more than the mere presence of depreciation. The statement places the term as the presentation introduces it after the P&L.

The statement is true.

EAR remains the simpler alternative, not double-entry bookkeeping. Sole proprietorships and partnerships under €700,000 turnover can prepare a receipts-and-payments account that is less elaborate than double-entry bookkeeping. Depreciation sits in the EAR; that does not make it double-entry bookkeeping with balance sheet, P&L and double profit determination. Corporations and exceeding the turnover threshold lead to double-entry bookkeeping. The statement mixes both forms.

The statement is false.

title: P&L of FunBike GmbH
context: Profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): sales revenues 70,656,000, material expense 53,175,000, personnel expense 7,900,000, depreciation 1,800,000, other operating expenses 2,875,000, EBIT 4,906,000, interest income 12,000, interest expense 99,000, financial result −87,000, result before tax 4,819,000, taxes 1,204,750, annual result 3,614,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: Earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) amount to €4,906,000.
Material expense clearly exceeds personnel expense.
The financial result amounts to −€87,000.
The annual result agrees with the profit of €3,614,250 reported in the balance sheet.
The annual result amounts to €4,906,000.
tactical_explanations:
After operating expenses stands EBIT. Sales revenues 70,656,000 minus material 53,175,000 minus personnel 7,900,000 minus depreciation 1,800,000 minus other operating expenses 2,875,000 yield 4,906,000. 70,656,000 − 53,175,000 = 17,481,000; 17,481,000 − 7,900,000 = 9,581,000; 9,581,000 − 1,800,000 = 7,781,000; 7,781,000 − 2,875,000 = 4,906,000. The theory reports exactly this result before interest and tax. Interest and tax are not yet deducted in this €4,906,000 figure. The financial result and the tax line follow afterwards and lead to the annual result. Anyone who swaps EBIT and profit skips exactly these two P&L stages.

The statement is true.

Parts and intermediates dominate the expense side. Material expense €53,175,000 stands against personnel expense €7,900,000. 53,175,000 is accordingly several times as large as 7,900,000; that fits a bicycle producer that buys in many components. The relation is immediately readable from the two lines without estimation. Anyone who held the personnel block for the largest expense would contradict the P&L. 53,175,000 to 7,900,000 is more than sixfold.

The statement is true.

Interest net with a sign. Interest income 12,000 minus interest expense 99,000 yield minus €87,000. The financial result is accordingly negative and separates EBIT from the result before tax. Anyone who confuses EBIT with the financial result reads the wrong line. The statement takes over the reported balance correctly. The negative financial result sits between EBIT and result before tax.

The statement is true.

The same €3,614,250 bridge between P&L and balance sheet. Annual result or profit €3,614,250 stands in the P&L; in the balance sheet the same profit appears in equity beside the cash contributions of €525,000. 4,819,000 − 1,204,750 = 3,614,250 confirms the tax line. The agreement is accordingly double profit determination in figures, not chance of two independent amounts.

The statement is true.

€4,906,000 is accordingly EBIT, not profit after interest and tax. After financial result −87,000 follows 4,819,000 before tax; after taxes 1,204,750 remains 3,614,250. Anyone who reads 4,906,000 as annual result stops before interest and tax. The P&L distinguishes the stages expressly. Profit in the balance sheet is 3,614,250, not 4,906,000.

The statement is false.

title: Cash flow and profit
context: Assess the following statements on the cash-flow statement:
statements: Published annual financial statements comprise, besides balance sheet and P&L, also a cash-flow statement.
The cash-flow statement shows cash inflows and cash outflows in a period and is also called the statement of cash flows.
One can achieve a profit without having liquid funds.
One can be liquid without achieving a profit.
Cash flow is identical with profit because both measure the same period result.
tactical_explanations:
Three parts form the published statements here. Published annual financial statements comprise, besides balance sheet and P&L, also a cash-flow statement. It supplements assets and performance with the cash flows. Investors find there whether the core business delivers cash surpluses. The statement lists the components as introduced after the FunBike P&L.

The statement is true.

Cash flow, not expense and income. The cash-flow statement shows the cash inflows and outflows into and out of the company over the period considered, usually for a financial year. That is why it is also called the statement of cash flows. Cash inflows and outflows stand at the centre, analogous to financial accounting, but structured by causes. The statement hits subject and alternative name.

The statement is true.

Profit without cash is possible. Cash flow is a ratio for solvency and not identical with profit; one can achieve a profit without having liquid funds. Receivables instead of payment, inventory build-up or repayment pressure can separate profit from liquidity. Depreciation reduces profit without cash outflow, while other events draw cash without hitting profit the same way. The statement holds exactly this possibility. FunBike's €1,800,000 depreciation reduces profit without cash having to flow out in the same amount.

The statement is true.

Cash without profit is likewise possible. One can be liquid without achieving a profit. Borrowing or selling non-current assets increase cash without the P&L therefore having to show profit. A loss year with still existing bank balances fits the same picture. The statement is the second half of the same distinction in the theory.

The statement is true.

Two ratios, two questions. Cash flow is not identical with profit. Profit answers whether the company became richer or poorer; cash flow answers the cash inflow and liquidity. The claim that both measure the same period result and are therefore identical erases depreciation, provisions, inventory and financing transactions. Exactly for that reason the cash-flow statement stands beside the P&L, not as a copy.

The statement is false.

title: Areas of the cash-flow statement
context: Assess the following statements on the areas of the cash-flow statement:
statements: The operating activities area is the most important in the cash-flow statement because it concerns the core of the business.
In the financing area, inflows can arise when new shareholders bring equity or loans bring debt capital.
Interest payments, dividend payments or loan repayments stand as an outflow in the financing area.
In the investing area, cash flows out when non-current assets are bought, and can flow in when, for example, land is sold.
Investors look primarily at the investing area because only there does the core of the business become visible.
tactical_explanations:
Operations hit the ongoing core. The operating activities area is the most important in the cash-flow statement because it concerns the core of the business. It shows whether cash surpluses are earned there. Investors therefore often look especially at this part. Financing and investing explain capital raising and asset purchases but do not replace the view of the operating business.

The statement is true.

New funds from shareholders or banks land under financing. This area shows inflows from financing activities when, for example, new shareholders and thus equity, or loans and thus debt capital, have been taken on. That is origin of funds in cash terms, not sales from bicycle sales. The statement correctly assigns both sources to this block.

The statement is true.

Financing outflows are interest, dividends and repayment. The outflow in this area stands, for example, in connection with interest payments, dividend payments or loan repayments. Those are capital costs and capital returns, not the purchase of a machine. Anyone who forces them into operating activities mixes core process and capital structure.

The statement is true.

Buying assets ties up cash; selling assets frees cash. In the investing area it shows whether cash has flowed into long-term investments to buy non-current assets. On the other hand cash can be generated when non-current assets have been sold — for example land or a building. Both concern long-term binding, not daily sales. The statement names inflow and outflow in the direction provided.

The statement is true.

The core sits in operating activities, not in investing. Investors often look especially at the operating activities part because there it becomes visible whether the core business delivers cash surpluses. The investing area explains asset purchases and sales, not the ongoing success of the business model. The claim swaps the most important area with another. Machine purchase can even stand negative in investing cash flow while the operating business is healthy. A strong negative investing cash flow can even be a sign of machine purchase and growth, while weak operating surpluses would be the real warning signal. The ranking of the three areas must therefore not be reversed.

The statement is false.

title: Current-asset intensity and golden balance-sheet rule
context: Balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, receivables 598,000, bank balances 320,250, balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: Assets meant to remain in the company longer than one year are called non-current assets — for example buildings and machines.
Current assets usually remain in the company for less than one year — for example inventories.
FunBike is current-asset intensive because current assets lie clearly above non-current assets.
The golden balance-sheet rule requires that long-term tied assets should also be financed long-term.
FunBike has clearly more non-current assets than current assets.
tactical_explanations:
Longer than one year — that is the threshold of non-current assets. Assets meant to remain in the company longer than one year are called non-current assets — for example buildings and machines. At FunBike, land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment 2,330,000 and financial assets 240,000 stand together at €3,320,000. That is long-term tied assets, not the stock of frames and tyres. The statement restates the maturity rule of the definition.

The statement is true.

Under one year lies current assets. They are the part of assets that usually remain in the company for less than one year — for example inventories. Receivables and bank balances belong in the same group. FunBike shows inventories 5,400,000, receivables 598,000 and bank 320,250. The statement hits definition and example without pushing inventories into non-current assets.

The statement is true.

Inventories make the business inventory- and current-asset heavy. Non-current assets 750,000 + 2,330,000 + 240,000 = €3,320,000. Current assets 5,400,000 + 598,000 + 320,250 = €6,318,250. 6,318,250 lies clearly above 3,320,000 — therefore current-asset intensive. For a bicycle producer with many components and finished bikes in stock that is plausible. Still, inventory holding could be checked for whether it is reducible without impairing production.

The statement is true.

Long binding needs long financing. The golden balance-sheet rule requires that long-term tied assets should also be financed long-term. At FunBike long-term assets lie somewhat above three million euro, equity over four million, and part of debt capital will presumably be long-term; the rule is met. Short-term trade payables alone must not carry the machine hall. Short-term trade payables of €300,000 could not carry technical equipment of over two million euro. Equity over four million plus presumably long-term bank loans fit the binding duration of non-current assets. The theory checks exactly this maturity congruence of financing, not a short-term liquidity ratio.

The statement is true.

The relation lies the other way. Current assets 6,318,250 against non-current assets 3,320,000: clearly more current than non-current assets. The claim that FunBike has clearly more non-current assets contradicts the additions and the label as current-asset intensive. Buildings and machines are large in euro; inventories are larger. Anyone who only reads the first assets line overlooks the inventory block.

The statement is false.

title: Capital structure of FunBike GmbH
context: Equity and liabilities of FunBike GmbH (euro): cash contributions 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000, total capital 9,638,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: Equity amounts to €4,139,250 and thus lies over four million euro.
Around 57 percent of capital is debt capital.
The bulk of debt capital falls on bank loans.
High dependence on debt capital is atypical for Austrian SMEs.
If the high profit remains in the company, it strengthens equity and internal financing power.
tactical_explanations:
Cash contributions plus profit yield equity. 525,000 + 3,614,250 = €4,139,250. The theory speaks of equity amounting to over four million euro; 4,139,250 lies clearly above. This amount, together with long-term debt capital, finances non-current assets in the sense of the golden balance-sheet rule. The €4,139,250 are not debt capital and not the balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Together with part of debt capital this equity finances non-current assets of somewhat more than three million euro and thus meets the golden balance-sheet rule.

The statement is true.

Debt capital divided by balance-sheet total. Provisions 2,000,000 + bank loans 3,199,000 + payables 300,000 = €5,499,000 debt capital. 5,499,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.5705, so around 57 percent. Exactly this share is named. Equity 4,139,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 43 percent is the remainder, not the majority of financing. 100 times 5,499,000 divided by 9,638,250 lies at 57.05 percent, rounded to the around 57 percent named.

The statement is true.

Credit line beats provisions and suppliers. Of €5,499,000 debt capital, 3,199,000 fall on bank loans, 2,000,000 on provisions and 300,000 on trade payables. 3,199,000 is the largest single item. As an example, the bulk of debt capital goes back to bank loans. Supplier credit of €300,000 does not carry the structure.

The statement is true.

For Austrian SMEs a high debt-capital ratio is typical. The capital structure with around 57 percent debt capital is not atypical for an Austrian company of this size; it is typical for Austrian SMEs to be highly dependent on debt capital. The claim that this is atypical reverses the sentence. FunBike with a balance-sheet total just under €10 million still counts among small enterprises and fits this picture.

The statement is false.

Retained profit is internal financing. The high profit strengthens equity and internal financing power if it remains in the company. €3,614,250 in equity is exactly this lever; distribution would reduce it again. Management must decide whether profit is withdrawn or left for machines and plant. The statement ties the strengthening to retention, not to every arising of profit regardless of use.

The statement is true.

title: FunBike: balance-sheet equality without looking up
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Assess the following statements:
statements: Total assets and total capital each amount to €9,638,250.
The sum of assets exceeds the sum of equity and liabilities by more than €500,000.
The shareholders' cash contributions alone are already the entire equity.
tactical_explanations:
Both sides close with the same figure. On the assets side one adds land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, receivables 598,000 and bank balances 320,250. Calculation: 750,000 + 2,330,000 = 3,080,000, plus 240,000 = 3,320,000, plus 5,400,000 = 8,720,000, plus 598,000 = 9,318,000, plus 320,250 = 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities: cash contributions 525,000 + profit 3,614,250 = 4,139,250, plus provisions 2,000,000 = 6,139,250, plus bank loans 3,199,000 = 9,338,250, plus payables 300,000 = 9,638,250. Assets equal capital, as the totals line of the definition shows.

The statement is true.

Equity stands in two equity-and-liability lines, not in one. Formula: equity = shareholders' cash contributions + profit. Insert from the definition: 525,000 + 3,614,250 = €4,139,250. Check against the balance-sheet total: debt capital 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 + 300,000 = 5,499,000, and 4,139,250 + 5,499,000 = 9,638,250. Anyone who only reads the cash contributions 525,000 omits the profit 3,614,250, which forms by far the larger part of own funds.

The statement is true.

There is no imbalance between the sides at FunBike. Sum of assets = 9,638,250, sum of equity and liabilities = 9,638,250. Difference: 9,638,250 − 9,638,250 = 0. The claim that assets lie more than 500,000 above equity and liabilities demands a gap the totals line does not give. In bookkeeping assets = capital: every part of the assets is accordingly financed; assets stand in debit, equity and liabilities in credit. A difference over 500,000 would break the balance sheet; FunBike shows debit–credit equality.

The statement is false.

Debt capital gathers three equity-and-liability positions below equity. Formula: debt capital = provisions + bank loans + trade payables. Insert: 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 = 5,199,000, plus 300,000 = €5,499,000. Check: total capital 9,638,250 minus equity 4,139,250 = 5,499,000. Bank loans 3,199,000 are the largest chunk (3,199,000 / 5,499,000 ≈ 0.58) but replace neither provisions nor trade payables.

The statement is true.

Not every contribution line is already the whole equity. Shareholders' cash contributions stand at 525,000 in the definition. Equity is 525,000 + profit 3,614,250 = 4,139,250. Comparison: 525,000 / 4,139,250 ≈ 0.127, so around 13 percent of own funds; profit carries the remaining 87 percent. The statement erases exactly the profit line and would make FunBike appear undercapitalised even though €4,139,250 of own funds stand on the equity-and-liabilities side.

The statement is false.

title: FunBike: non-current and current assets
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Assets meant to remain tied longer than one year count as non-current assets; shorter-tied assets as current assets. Assess the following statements:
statements: Non-current assets clearly exceed current assets.
FunBike is current-asset intensive because current assets lie clearly above non-current assets.
Within current assets, inventories dominate at €5,400,000.
tactical_explanations:
Tied longer than one year: those are the three non-current lines. Formula: non-current assets = land and buildings + technical equipment and office equipment + financial assets. Insert: 750,000 + 2,330,000 = 3,080,000, plus 240,000 = €3,320,000. The theory here counts buildings and machines as non-current assets, inventories expressly not. Check against the balance-sheet total: 9,638,250 − 3,320,000 = 6,318,250 remains for current assets. The €3,320,000 are the long-term assets of somewhat more than three million of which the golden balance-sheet rule later speaks.

The statement is true.

Shorter than one year: inventories, receivables, bank balances. Formula: current assets = inventories + trade receivables + bank balances and cash. Insert: 5,400,000 + 598,000 = 5,998,000, plus 320,250 = €6,318,250. Check: non-current 3,320,000 + current 6,318,250 = 9,638,250 closes the assets side without remainder. Inventories 5,400,000 alone already carry the bulk of this current block; receivables and bank are the smaller remainders 598,000 and 320,250.

The statement is true.

The relation lies opposite to the claim. Comparison from the definition: current assets 6,318,250 against non-current assets 3,320,000. Difference: 6,318,250 − 3,320,000 = €2,998,250 in favour of current assets. Ratio: 6,318,250 / 3,320,000 ≈ 1.90, so nearly double. Anyone who reads buildings and machines as the larger block overlooks the inventories line 5,400,000, which alone already lies above all non-current assets (5,400,000 > 3,320,000). FunBike is therefore not fixed-asset heavy.

The statement is false.

Current-asset intensive means: clearly more current than non-current assets. Figures of the definition: 6,318,250 stands against 3,320,000, so more than 1.9 times (6,318,250 / 3,320,000 ≈ 1.90). Share of total assets: 6,318,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.656, around 66 percent current. The theory classifies FunBike exactly so, because a bicycle producer stocks components and finished bikes. The machine hall 2,330,000 does not change this classification as long as inventories carry the current block.

The statement is true.

Inventories stand out from current assets. Current assets = 6,318,250, of which inventories 5,400,000. Share: 5,400,000 / 6,318,250 ≈ 0.855, so around 86 percent. Remainder: receivables 598,000 + bank 320,250 = 918,250. For a bicycle producer that stocks many parts and partly finished bikes that is plausible. Still, one could check whether inventory holding is reducible without impairing production. Dominance here means: one line carries almost the whole current block.

The statement is true.

title: FunBike: equity, debt capital, ratio
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Assess the following statements on financing:
statements: Around 57 percent of capital is debt capital.
The equity ratio lies above 60 percent of the balance-sheet total.
The bulk of debt capital is formed by bank loans at €3,199,000.
Equity amounts to over four million euro.
All debt capital consists only of the trade payables of €300,000.
tactical_explanations:
Debt-capital ratio needs numerator and denominator from the definition. Numerator: provisions 2,000,000 + bank loans 3,199,000 + payables 300,000 = 5,499,000. Denominator: balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Quotient: 5,499,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.5705, so around 57 percent. Check: equity 4,139,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.4295, and 57.05 + 42.95 = 100 percent. Bank loans alone are 3,199,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 33 percent of the balance-sheet total and drive the ratio. Exactly this order of magnitude is named for FunBike and held not atypical for an Austrian company just under €10 million balance-sheet total.

The statement is true.

Sixty percent equity does not fit these figures. Equity = 525,000 + 3,614,250 = 4,139,250. Ratio: 4,139,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.4295, so around 43 percent, not over 60. The 60-percent threshold of 9,638,250 would be 5,782,950; 4,139,250 remains 1,643,700 below. 43 percent lies clearly under 60; the claim twists equity and debt shares. FunBike finances itself predominantly with debt (5,499,000 against 4,139,250), not three-fifths with equity.

The statement is false.

Bank loans against the remaining debt. Debt capital 5,499,000, of which bank loans 3,199,000. Share: 3,199,000 / 5,499,000 ≈ 0.582, so around 58 percent. Provisions 2,000,000 plus suppliers 300,000 together yield 2,300,000, less than the bank line alone. 3,199,000 > 2,300,000, therefore the bulk. As an example, the bulk of debt capital goes back to bank loans; the three debt lines of the definition confirm that without further assumptions.

The statement is true.

Four-million threshold and balance-sheet value. Equity = cash contributions 525,000 + profit 3,614,250 = €4,139,250. Comparison: 4,139,250 > 4,000,000, difference 139,250. The theory speaks of equity amounting to over four million euro. Exactly this buffer carries the golden balance-sheet rule, because long-term assets are only 3,320,000 — somewhat over three million. 4,139,250 − 3,320,000 = 819,250 over-coverage by own funds.

The statement is true.

Three hundred thousand do not replace 5.5 million. Trade payables stand at 300,000 in a single line. Debt capital additionally comprises provisions 2,000,000 and bank loans 3,199,000, total 5,499,000. Share of suppliers: 300,000 / 5,499,000 ≈ 0.055, barely 5.5 percent, not the whole. Anyone who only reads the last equity-and-liability line omits bank and provisions and would make FunBike appear almost debt-free.

The statement is false.

title: FunBike: golden balance-sheet rule
