context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Long-term tied assets should be financed with matching maturities. Assess the following statements:
statements: The long-term assets of €3,320,000 are more than covered by equity of €4,139,250; the golden balance-sheet rule is met.
Because 3,320,000 is greater than 4,139,250, FunBike breaches the golden balance-sheet rule.
Inventories of €5,400,000 count as non-current assets because they are indispensable for production.
Trade payables of €300,000 alone finance the technical equipment of €2,330,000 with matching maturities.
Part of debt capital can additionally be long-term and further support coverage of non-current assets.
tactical_explanations:
Maturity congruence is checked numerically on the definition. Long-term assets = non-current assets = 750,000 + 2,330,000 + 240,000 = €3,320,000 (somewhat more than three million, as stated). Equity = 525,000 + 3,614,250 = €4,139,250 (over four million). Comparison: 4,139,250 > 3,320,000, over-coverage €819,250. Thus long-term tied assets are already fully financed by own funds. The golden balance-sheet rule — that long-term assets should be financed long-term — is met even before one adds a presumably long-term part of debt capital.

The statement is true.

The inequality stands the wrong way round. 3,320,000 is not greater than 4,139,250 but smaller: 4,139,250 − 3,320,000 = 819,250. Anyone who presents the golden balance-sheet rule as breached swaps assets and capital. It is expressly established that the rule is met, because long-term assets lie somewhat over three million and equity over four million. A breached rule would exist if 3,320,000 stood uncovered above long-term funds; here the opposite is the case.

The statement is false.

Indispensable does not yet make non-current assets. The maturity rule: assets meant to remain in the company longer than one year are called non-current assets — for example buildings and machines. Inventories usually remain shorter than one year and stand in the definition under current assets at 5,400,000. 5,400,000 therefore does not belong to the 3,320,000 non-current (750,000 + 2,330,000 + 240,000). Production closeness does not change the balance-sheet classification: frames and tyres in stock are current; the assembly hall is non-current. Classification follows planned dwell time, not operational importance.

The statement is false.

Three hundred thousand do not carry 2.33 million with matching maturities. Technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000 are non-current assets — that is, long-term tied. Trade payables 300,000 are typically short-term. Coverage: 300,000 / 2,330,000 ≈ 0.129, barely 13 percent of the equipment line, not full financing. Shortfall 2,330,000 − 300,000 = 2,030,000. The golden balance-sheet rule requires long-term coverage by equity 4,139,250 and presumably long-term parts of debt capital, not by supplier terms alone.

The statement is false.

Equity suffices; additional long-term debt would be a reserve. It holds: equity amounts to over four million and part of debt capital will presumably also be long-term. Bank loans 3,199,000 can have maturities over one year; provisions 2,000,000 are not automatically short-term. Even without this presumption, equity 4,139,250 already covers non-current assets 3,320,000 (overhang 819,250). The statement stays within the framework: it invents no second firm, no second year and no figure outside the definition.

The statement is true.

title: FunBike: P&L from sales to EBIT
context: Profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): sales revenues 70,656,000, material expense 53,175,000, personnel expense 7,900,000, depreciation 1,800,000, other operating expenses 2,875,000, earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) 4,906,000, interest income 12,000, interest expense 99,000, financial result −87,000, result before tax 4,819,000, taxes 1,204,750, annual result 3,614,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: Sales revenues minus the four operating expense blocks yield EBIT of €4,906,000.
The financial result amounts to 12,000 − 99,000 = −€87,000.
The annual result is identical with EBIT of €4,906,000.
Result before tax = EBIT + financial result = 4,906,000 + (−87,000) = €4,819,000.
Taxes of €1,204,750 exceed the profit of €3,614,250.
tactical_explanations:
Operating result is calculated line by line. Start: sales revenues 70,656,000. Minus material 53,175,000 yields 17,481,000. Minus personnel 7,900,000 yields 9,581,000. Minus depreciation 1,800,000 yields 7,781,000. Minus other operating expenses 2,875,000 yields 4,906,000. That is accordingly exactly the EBIT line of the definition. Check in one step: sum of the four expenses 53,175,000 + 7,900,000 + 1,800,000 + 2,875,000 = 65,750,000, and 70,656,000 − 65,750,000 = 4,906,000. Interest 12,000 and 99,000 and taxes 1,204,750 do not yet belong in this stage; they come only after EBIT.

The statement is true.

Interest has a sign and a netting. Formula: financial result = interest income − interest expense. Insert from the definition: 12,000 − 99,000 = −€87,000. The financial-result line reports exactly these −87,000. Interest expense exceeds interest income by 87,000; the balance is accordingly negative and reduces the result after EBIT 4,906,000 to 4,819,000 before tax. The financial result replaces neither EBIT nor the annual result; it is the interest bridge in between.

The statement is true.

EBIT is accordingly an intermediate stage, not profit after interest and tax. After EBIT 4,906,000 follows financial result −87,000, then 4,819,000 before tax, then taxes 1,204,750, then annual result 3,614,250. Comparison: 4,906,000 ≠ 3,614,250. Difference 4,906,000 − 3,614,250 = 1,291,750 — that is exactly financial result 87,000 plus taxes 1,204,750. Anyone who reads EBIT as annual result stops two lines too early. In the balance sheet, profit stands at 3,614,250, not 4,906,000.

The statement is false.

The bridge from operating result to the tax base. Formula: result before tax = EBIT + financial result. Insert: 4,906,000 + (−87,000) = 4,819,000. The threshold confirms 4,819,000. Check backwards: 4,819,000 − 4,906,000 = −87,000, equal to the financial result. Without this identity the P&L would be internally inconsistent; with it the next subtraction — taxes 1,204,750 — sits on the right base and leads to 3,614,250.

The statement is true.

Do not swap tax line and profit line. Comparison in the definition: taxes 1,204,750 against annual result 3,614,250. 1,204,750 < 3,614,250, difference 3,614,250 − 1,204,750 = 2,409,500. Check of the profit line: result before tax 4,819,000 − taxes 1,204,750 = 3,614,250. Taxes are the deduction from the tax base, not the larger remainder. The statement asserts the opposite of the two last P&L figures and would read profit as smaller than the tax burden.

The statement is false.

title: FunBike: profit in P&L and balance sheet
context: Profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): sales revenues 70,656,000, material expense 53,175,000, personnel expense 7,900,000, depreciation 1,800,000, other operating expenses 2,875,000, earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) 4,906,000, interest income 12,000, interest expense 99,000, financial result −87,000, result before tax 4,819,000, taxes 1,204,750, annual result 3,614,250. In the balance sheet stand cash contributions 525,000 and profit 3,614,250. Assess the following statements on double profit determination:
statements: The P&L annual result of €3,614,250 is the same amount as the profit in the balance sheet.
Equity = cash contributions 525,000 + P&L profit 3,614,250 = €4,139,250.
In the balance sheet the sales-revenues line of €70,656,000 stands as profit.
Material expense €53,175,000 is the annual result.
4,819,000 − 1,204,750 = 3,614,250 closes the P&L and binds the balance-sheet profit.
tactical_explanations:
Two disclosures, one figure. The P&L ends with annual result / profit 3,614,250. In the balance sheet under equity stands the profit line 3,614,250. Comparison: 3,614,250 = 3,614,250. Check of the last P&L stage: 4,819,000 − 1,204,750 = 3,614,250. Exactly that is what double profit determination means: profit is determined in the P&L and must also result from the equity comparison — both the same amount. Were the amounts different, double-entry bookkeeping in these FunBike figures would be broken. Balance sheet and P&L are therefore not two independent stories but one identity.

The statement is true.

The equity-and-liabilities side takes up the P&L profit. Formula: equity = shareholders' cash contributions + profit. The profit is accordingly the annual result 3,614,250 from the P&L. Insert: 525,000 + 3,614,250 = €4,139,250. Check against the balance-sheet total: debt capital 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 + 300,000 = 5,499,000, and 4,139,250 + 5,499,000 = 9,638,250. Profit increases equity if it remains in the company; balance sheet and P&L already show it at this height.

The statement is true.

Sales is accordingly the first P&L line, not the balance-sheet profit line. Sales revenues 70,656,000 stand only at the top of the income statement. In the balance sheet the profit position reads 3,614,250. Comparison: 70,656,000 ≠ 3,614,250. In between lie material 53,175,000, personnel 7,900,000, depreciation 1,800,000, other expenses 2,875,000, financial result 87,000 and taxes 1,204,750. Anyone who copies sales into equity and liabilities confuses revenues with the period result after all deductions and would break the balance-sheet total.

The statement is false.

Material is accordingly expense, not profit. Material expense 53,175,000 is the largest minus line of the P&L. Annual result is 3,614,250. Comparison: 53,175,000 ≠ 3,614,250; the material block is even larger than EBIT 4,906,000. Share of sales: 53,175,000 / 70,656,000 ≈ 0.753 — around 75 percent of revenues go into material. The remainder carries personnel, depreciation, other expenses, interest, taxes and only then the profit 3,614,250 that returns in the balance sheet.

The statement is false.

Last subtraction before profit. Formula: annual result = result before tax − taxes. Insert: 4,819,000 − 1,204,750 = 3,614,250. The same 3,614,250 stands in the balance sheet as profit beside the cash contributions 525,000. The chain sits throughout: EBIT 4,906,000 plus financial result −87,000 yields 4,819,000, minus taxes 1,204,750 yields 3,614,250. Thus the bridge between profit and loss statement and balance sheet is arithmetically closed, as double profit determination requires.

The statement is true.

title: FunBike: current-asset intensity and asset shares
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Assess the following statements:
statements: Inventories of €5,400,000 by themselves exceed total non-current assets of €3,320,000.
More than half of the balance-sheet total is non-current assets.
Current assets make up more than 65 percent of the balance-sheet total.
Bank balances and cash €320,250 exceed inventories €5,400,000.
FunBike is current-asset intensive because €6,318,250 current assets lie clearly above €3,320,000 non-current assets and inventories dominate this current block.
tactical_explanations:
A single assets line beats the whole non-current block. Inventories 5,400,000, non-current assets 750,000 + 2,330,000 + 240,000 = 3,320,000. Comparison: 5,400,000 − 3,320,000 = €2,080,000 lead for inventories. Ratio: 5,400,000 / 3,320,000 ≈ 1.63 — a good 1.6 times all buildings, equipment and financial assets. Share of the balance-sheet total: 5,400,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.56 — so around 56 percent of total assets lie in inventory. Exactly for that reason the theory speaks of inventory dominance at a bicycle producer that stocks components and finished bikes.

The statement is true.

Non-current assets are accordingly the smaller part of assets. Share: 3,320,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.3444 — around 34 percent, not over 50 percent. Half the balance-sheet total would be 9,638,250 / 2 = 4,819,125; 3,320,000 remains 1,499,125 below. Current 6,318,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.656 lies clearly over half. Anyone who reads buildings and machines as majority assets ignores inventories 5,400,000 plus receivables 598,000 plus bank 320,250. The definition is current-asset heavy, not fixed-asset heavy.

The statement is false.

Sixty-five percent as threshold against the calculated value. Current assets = 5,400,000 + 598,000 + 320,250 = 6,318,250. Ratio: 6,318,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 0.6556 — so around 65.6 percent. Comparison to the threshold: 65.6 > 65; the condition is accordingly met. Check: non-current 3,320,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 34.4 percent, and 34.4 + 65.6 = 100 percent of the 9,638,250. The statement requires exactly this reading of the three current lines, not an estimate without division.

The statement is true.

Cash against warehouse: the order of magnitude tips. Bank balances and cash 320,250, inventories 5,400,000. Comparison: 320,250 < 5,400,000. Ratio: 320,250 / 5,400,000 ≈ 0.059 — around 6 percent of inventories. Difference 5,400,000 − 320,250 = 5,079,750. Liquid funds exist but dominate neither current assets (6,318,250) nor the balance-sheet total (9,638,250). The claim swaps the two lines and would make FunBike appear cash-heavy instead of inventory-intensive.

The statement is false.

Both criteria jointly apply at FunBike. Current 6,318,250 against non-current 3,320,000: 6,318,250 / 3,320,000 ≈ 1.90 — clearly more current, therefore current-asset intensive. Within current assets: inventories 5,400,000 / 6,318,250 ≈ 0.855 — around 86 percent, therefore inventory dominance. Receivables and bank remain 598,000 + 320,250 = 918,250. The theory applies exactly these two observations to FunBike without needing a second company or a second year.

The statement is true.

title: FunBike: ratios from balance sheet and P&L
context: The simplified balance sheet of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): Assets — land and buildings 750,000, technical equipment and office equipment 2,330,000, financial assets 240,000, inventories 5,400,000, trade receivables 598,000, bank balances and cash 320,250; balance-sheet total 9,638,250. Equity and liabilities — cash contributions by the shareholders 525,000, profit 3,614,250, provisions 2,000,000, bank loans 3,199,000, trade payables 300,000. Profit and loss statement of FunBike GmbH as at 31.12.20xx (euro): sales revenues 70,656,000, material expense 53,175,000, personnel expense 7,900,000, depreciation 1,800,000, other operating expenses 2,875,000, earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) 4,906,000, interest income 12,000, interest expense 99,000, financial result −87,000, result before tax 4,819,000, taxes 1,204,750, annual result 3,614,250. Assess the following statements:
statements: Debt-capital ratio = 5,499,000 / 9,638,250 ≈ 57 percent, as typical for FunBike.
Material expense corresponds to more than 70 percent of sales revenues.
Personnel expense €7,900,000 exceeds material expense €53,175,000.
The profit €3,614,250 in the balance sheet is smaller than EBIT €4,906,000 because afterwards financial result and taxes are still deducted.
Depreciation €1,800,000 is in the same period a cash-outflow amount of equal height and therefore identical with profit.
tactical_explanations:
Ratio from equity and liabilities, not from feeling. Debt capital = 2,000,000 + 3,199,000 + 300,000 = 5,499,000. Balance-sheet total = 9,638,250. Division: 5,499,000 / 9,638,250 = 0.570539… ≈ 57.05 percent, rounded as around 57 percent. Check equity ratio: (525,000 + 3,614,250) / 9,638,250 = 4,139,250 / 9,638,250 ≈ 42.95 percent, and 57.05 + 42.95 = 100. The capital structure with around 57 percent debt capital, of which the bulk bank loans 3,199,000, thus remains pinned to the thresholds.

The statement is true.

Measure material intensity on sales. Numerator material expense 53,175,000, denominator sales revenues 70,656,000. Quotient: 53,175,000 / 70,656,000 ≈ 0.7526 — so around 75.3 percent. Comparison to the threshold: 75.3 > 70; the condition is clearly met. Personnel 7,900,000 / 70,656,000 ≈ 0.112 — around 11.2 percent — remains far below. Depreciation 1,800,000 / 70,656,000 ≈ 2.5 percent. For the bicycle producer the material block is the dominant operating expense; the profit and loss statement shows that in the first minus line.

The statement is true.

Personnel against material: the larger line is material. Comparison of the P&L: personnel expense 7,900,000 against material expense 53,175,000. 7,900,000 − 53,175,000 = −45,275,000 — personnel lies €45.275 million under material. Ratio: 7,900,000 / 53,175,000 ≈ 0.149 — around 15 percent of material expense. The statement flips the two minus lines. EBIT 4,906,000 arises only after the much larger material deduction has already been taken from sales revenues 70,656,000.

The statement is false.

Profit after interest and tax is the smaller stage. EBIT 4,906,000, annual result 3,614,250, and exactly 3,614,250 stands in the balance sheet as profit. Difference: 4,906,000 − 3,614,250 = 1,291,750. Breakdown on the P&L: financial result 87,000 plus taxes 1,204,750 = 1,291,750. Stages: EBIT 4,906,000, result before tax 4,819,000, annual result 3,614,250. Therefore the balance-sheet profit must lie under EBIT once interest and taxes book negatively. Balance sheet and P&L carry the same 3,614,250.

The statement is true.

Depreciation is expense, not automatically a cash outflow and not the profit. The P&L shows depreciation −1,800,000 and annual result 3,614,250; comparison 1,800,000 ≠ 3,614,250. The presentation on financial accounting names depreciation as an example that an expenditure need not be accompanied by a cash outflow. Profit and cash flow are not identical: one can achieve a profit without having liquid funds, and be liquid without achieving a profit. FunBike illustrates the separation because 1,800,000 reduce profit without cash having to flow out in the same amount. Cash inflows and outflows are steered by financial or cash-flow accounting; income and expenses by the P&L.

The statement is false.

title: Unit contribution margin from price and variable costs
context: A bicycle producer sells a model at €400 per unit; variable costs are €180 per unit. Assess the following statements on the unit contribution margin:
statements: The contribution margin per bike results as price minus variable costs — that is, 400 minus 180 equals €220.
The contribution margin per bike is €180 because that is the variable costs.
The contribution ratio is 220 divided by 400 — that is, 55 percent.
The contribution ratio is 180 divided by 400 — that is, 45 percent.
The selling price exceeds variable costs by €220 per bike.
tactical_explanations:
Price minus variable costs per unit. €400 selling price less €180 variable costs yield €220 unit contribution margin. This amount remains after deducting quantity costs to carry the fixed costs. It is neither the price nor the variable costs alone. The difference is the central figure of the break-even calculation.

The statement is true.

One hundred and eighty are costs, not contribution margin. Variable costs per bike are €180; the contribution margin is the difference from the price: 400 minus 180 equals €220. Anyone who sets 180 as contribution margin confuses the cost block with the surplus per unit. Fixed-cost coverage starts only at the €220. Only the difference from the price of €400 yields the contribution margin.

The statement is false.

Two hundred and twenty of four hundred are 55 percent. The contribution ratio sets the unit contribution margin in relation to the price: 220 divided by 400 yields 0.55. Of every euro of sales, 55 cents remain for fixed-cost coverage. The ratio is a relative figure, not a euro amount. It later steers break-even sales.

The statement is true.

Forty-five percent is the variable-cost share. 180 divided by 400 yields 0.45; that is the share of variable costs in the price, not the contribution ratio. The contribution ratio is 220 divided by 400 equals 0.55. Anyone who swaps cost share and contribution ratio underestimates the contribution to fixed-cost coverage. The contribution ratio lies at 55 percent, not at this cost share.

The statement is false.

This point: price lies €220 above quantity costs. 400 minus 180 yields the same surplus per bike that as unit contribution margin helps carry fixed costs. Without this gap nothing would remain for fixed costs and profit. The statement describes exactly this difference. It is the verbal form of the contribution-margin formula. Without this gap nothing would remain for fixed costs and later profit.

The statement is true.

title: Break-even sales from fixed costs and contribution ratio
context: The same bicycle producer carries €4,000,000 fixed costs per year; the contribution margin per bike is €220 at a selling price of €400. Assess the following statements on break-even sales:
statements: Break-even sales result from dividing the fixed costs of €4,000,000 by the contribution ratio of 0.55.
At a contribution ratio of 55 percent the company must achieve more than €4,000,000 in sales to cover all costs.
Break-even sales correspond exactly to the fixed costs of €4,000,000 because the fixed costs determine the sales threshold.
Break-even sales result from multiplying the fixed costs by the contribution ratio 0.55.
Above break-even sales the company achieves a profit because the fixed costs are then already covered.
tactical_explanations:
Fixed costs divided by the ratio. At the break-even point the cumulative contribution margins just cover the fixed costs: sales times 0.55 equals 4,000,000, so sales equal 4,000,000 divided by 0.55 — around €7,272,727. Division by the contribution ratio delivers exactly this threshold. Without the ratio only the fixed-cost figure would remain.

The statement is true.

Four million sales do not suffice at 55 percent. Only 55 cents of each sales euro contribute to fixed-cost coverage; 4,000,000 times 0.55 would be only €2,200,000 contribution margin. The needed sales lie clearly above — at around €7.27 million. Therefore the company must achieve more than €4,000,000 in sales. The statement hits this under-coverage logic.

The statement is true.

Fixed costs and break-even sales are not identical. Only at a contribution ratio of 100 percent would both coincide. At 55 percent sales must be larger than the fixed costs themselves: 4,000,000 divided by 0.55 yields around €7,272,727, not 4,000,000. Anyone who equates both ignores the variable-cost share. At a 55 percent ratio the threshold lies clearly above pure fixed costs.

The statement is false.

Multiplying delivers the contribution margin of an already known sales figure, not the sought break-even sales. 4,000,000 × 0.55 = 2,200,000 would be the contribution at sales of €4 million — far under the fixed costs to be covered. What is sought is the inverse: division instead of multiplication.

The statement is false.

Above the threshold contribution margin becomes profit. Every euro of sales above continues to deliver 55 cents contribution that is no longer needed for fixed costs, because those are already covered. Below the threshold fixed costs remain partly uncovered. The profit zone begins only from break-even sales. Proximity alone does not suffice.

The statement is true.

title: Interpreting the contribution ratio correctly
context: The same bicycle producer calculates with €400 selling price, €180 variable costs and €4,000,000 fixed costs per year. Assess the following statements on the contribution ratio:
statements: The contribution ratio states what percent of each selling-price euro remains for fixed-cost coverage after deducting variable costs.
The contribution ratio can be calculated by dividing fixed costs by the selling price of a single unit.
At the break-even point the contribution ratio multiplied by break-even sales exactly meets the fixed costs.
The contribution ratio is to be equated with variable costs per unit in euro.
The higher the contribution ratio, the lower the needed break-even sales at the same fixed costs.
tactical_explanations:
The ratio measures the remainder per sales euro. After deducting variable costs a percentage remains for fixed-cost coverage; that is accordingly the contribution ratio. It is the relation of contribution margin to selling price, not an absolute euro amount. Anyone who confuses it with fixed costs or unit counts reads the wrong figure. The statement hits the interpretation.

The statement is true.

Fixed costs divided by unit price yield a quantity, not a percentage. The contribution ratio arises from contribution margin divided by selling price and does not hang on the absolute height of fixed costs. Anyone who divides fixed costs by €400 calculates a piece-count-like figure and misses the ratio. The correct numerator is accordingly the contribution margin.

The statement is false.

At break-even, ratio times sales meets fixed costs. By definition: contribution ratio multiplied by break-even sales equals fixed costs. Exactly there the cumulative contribution margins offset the fixed costs without profit or loss. The statement describes this zero-profit condition. It is accordingly the check of the break-even calculation.

The statement is true.

Variable costs are a money amount per unit; the contribution ratio by contrast is a percentage of the selling price. Both figures hang together but are not identical: the ratio describes which share of the price remains after deducting variable costs, not the variable costs themselves.

The statement is false.

A higher ratio lowers the needed sales. Because break-even sales equal fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio, the denominator becomes larger and the result smaller when the ratio rises. At the same fixed costs less sales then suffice for coverage. Anyone who raises the ratio shifts the threshold downwards. The statement hits this inverse.

The statement is true.

title: Determining the break-even unit quantity
context: From selling price €400, variable costs €180 and fixed costs €4,000,000 one can also derive the break-even unit quantity. Assess the following statements:
statements: The break-even unit quantity results from dividing fixed costs by the unit contribution margin.
The break-even unit quantity results from dividing fixed costs by the selling price.
If one multiplies the break-even unit quantity by the selling price, one obtains the same amount as for break-even sales via the contribution ratio.
If a company sells so many units that the fixed costs alone would be covered by the variable costs, that already suffices for break-even.
If a company sells more units than the break-even unit quantity, the cumulative contribution margin lies above the fixed costs.
tactical_explanations:
Each unit delivers the same contribution. Fixed costs are covered once the sum of unit contribution margins reaches the fixed costs. Formula: unit quantity equals fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. That is the quantity threshold in units, not in euro. Anyone who divides by the price instead of the contribution margin lands at the wrong quantity.

The statement is true.

This point: selling price alone does not cover fixed costs because variable costs per unit must first be deducted from it. The correct denominator is the contribution margin per unit (price minus variable costs), not the full selling price. Division by the price would understate the unit quantity.

The statement is false.

Unit path and sales path meet. Break-even unit quantity times selling price yields the same break-even sales as fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio. Both paths describe the same point in different units. The check: sales times ratio again yields the fixed costs. Anyone who obtains diverging thresholds has switched the denominator along the way.

The statement is true.

Variable costs are already accounted for in the contribution margin and themselves contribute nothing to fixed-cost coverage; they are precisely deducted before the contribution margin arises. Sales that only cover variable costs leave nothing for fixed costs and therefore do not suffice for break-even.

The statement is false.

Above the unit threshold profit arises. Each additional unit continues to deliver the same contribution margin that is now no longer needed for fixed costs, because those have already been reached. The cumulative contribution margin exceeds the fixed costs. Below the threshold under-coverage remains. More units than break-even therefore means the profit zone.

The statement is true.

title: Checking various sales levels for cost coverage
context: Using selling price €400, variable costs €180 and fixed costs €4,000,000, check whether selected annual sales cover the fixed costs. Assess the following statements:
statements: At annual sales equal to the fixed costs themselves, the fixed costs remain under-covered as long as the contribution ratio lies under 100 percent.
Annual sales equal to the fixed costs already lie at the break-even point.
Annual sales twice as high as the fixed costs necessarily lead into the profit zone.
Whether particular annual sales cover the fixed costs depends both on the sales themselves and on the contribution ratio.
Annual sales just under break-even sales already lie in the profit zone because they are close to the threshold.
tactical_explanations:
Sales equal to fixed costs do not suffice at a ratio under 100 percent. From sales the variable-cost share is first deducted; the remaining contribution margin then lies under the fixed costs. The fixed costs remain under-covered. Only higher sales close the gap. The statement describes exactly this under-coverage at a ratio under one.

The statement is true.

Break-even is fixed costs divided by the ratio, not the fixed costs themselves. At a ratio under 100 percent the actual break-even sales lie above the fixed costs because the denominator is smaller than one. Sales equal to the fixed costs are therefore not yet the break-even point. The statement wrongly equates both amounts.

The statement is false.

Sales lying far above break-even sales generate a contribution margin that exceeds the fixed costs — provided the contribution ratio remains positive, which is the case under realistic cost structures. Sales twice as high as the fixed costs generally clearly suffice for that.

The statement is true.

Cost coverage needs sales and ratio. Only sales times contribution ratio yields the contribution margin achieved, which is compared with the fixed costs. Sales alone, without knowledge of the ratio, say nothing yet about coverage. Both figures belong together. The statement holds exactly this two-stage nature. Without the ratio, sales alone stay silent on cost coverage.

The statement is true.

Just under the threshold is not yet the profit zone. Fixed costs are fully covered only from break-even sales. Proximity to the threshold does not mean it has already been reached. Below, a remainder of fixed costs stays open. Anyone who reads 'just under' as profit confuses approaching with exceeding. Only reaching or exceeding the threshold opens the profit zone.

The statement is false.

title: Calculation identities of break-even analysis
context: A bicycle producer calculates with selling price €400, variable costs €180 per unit and fixed costs of €4,000,000 per year. Assess the following statements on the calculation relationships:
statements: Contribution margin plus variable costs again yield the selling price per unit.
Break-even sales multiplied by the contribution ratio yield the fixed costs.
At the break-even point the sum of contribution margins equals the fixed costs.
At the break-even point sales correspond to the fixed costs, independently of the contribution ratio.
In the long run the selling price should cover not only the variable but also the fixed costs per unit.
tactical_explanations:
Contribution margin and variable costs form the price. Adding variable costs to the contribution margin returns the original selling price. The inverse confirms that both parts exhaust the price. If either is missing, the decomposition does not fit. The statement checks exactly this identity.

The statement is true.

Sales times ratio equal fixed costs at break-even. This check confirms that dividing fixed costs by the ratio delivers exactly the sales whose contribution margins meet the fixed costs. If the product diverges, the threshold is accordingly wrongly calculated. The identity is the defining zero-profit condition.

The statement is true.

Zero profit means: contribution margins equal fixed costs. No more and no less. That holds independently of whether one expresses the point via unit quantity or sales. Below, contribution is missing; above, profit arises. The statement hits the defining property of the break-even point.

The statement is true.

Sales equal fixed costs only at a 100 percent ratio. At every lower ratio sales must be larger than the fixed costs themselves for the contribution margins to reach them. The statement asserts independence from the ratio and is therefore false. Without the ratio the denominator of the break-even formula is missing.

The statement is false.

In the long run the price must carry both cost blocks. The contribution margin exists to finance fixed costs beyond variable costs. If the price permanently covers only quantity costs, fixed costs remain unpaid. Securing existence therefore demands coverage of both blocks. The statement holds this long-term rule.

The statement is true.

title: Correct and incorrect denominators in the break-even calculation
context: Selling price €400, variable costs €180 per unit, fixed costs €4,000,000: check which calculation paths actually hit break-even sales. Assess the following statements:
statements: Break-even sales can be calculated correctly by dividing fixed costs by the unit contribution margin and multiplying the result by the selling price.
Break-even sales can be calculated correctly by dividing fixed costs by the contribution ratio.
The contribution ratio can be calculated correctly by dividing the selling price by the variable costs.
To obtain the contribution ratio one first calculates the contribution margin as price minus variable costs and then divides it by the price.
Break-even sales can be calculated correctly by dividing fixed costs by the variable costs per unit.
tactical_explanations:
Unit quantity times price yields the sales path. Fixed costs divided by unit contribution margin deliver the break-even unit quantity; multiplied by the selling price the break-even sales in euro arise. Both steps together lead correctly to the target. Anyone who leaves out one step stays at units or at a wrong euro figure.

The statement is true.

Direct path via the ratio. Fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio immediately yield break-even sales, because at the break-even point sales times ratio equal fixed costs. That saves the detour via unit quantity. Prerequisite is the correct ratio from contribution margin and price. The statement names exactly this direct path.

The statement is true.

Price divided by variable costs is the wrong ratio. This division measures how often the quantity costs fit into the price, not the share of contribution margin in the price. The contribution ratio is contribution margin divided by price. Anyone who swaps numerator and denominator or takes the cost amount instead of the contribution misses the ratio.

The statement is false.

First difference, then share. The contribution margin arises as price minus variable costs; divided by the price it becomes the contribution ratio. This sequence delivers the correct ratio. Anyone who swaps the steps or chooses other denominators lands at a different ratio. The statement describes the definition in two stages correctly.

The statement is true.

Variable costs are the wrong denominator. They are precisely deducted from the price to obtain the contribution margin that carries the fixed costs. The correct unit denominator is the contribution margin; the correct sales denominator is the contribution ratio. Anyone who divides by €180 calculates no break-even threshold. The statement chooses the cost block instead of the contribution.

The statement is false.

title: Break-even check and securing existence
context: A bicycle producer knows selling price €400, variable costs €180 per unit and fixed costs €4,000,000 per year. Assess the following statements on the break-even check and securing existence:
statements: Calculated by units (fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit) and calculated by sales (fixed costs divided by contribution ratio, then by the price) lead to the same break-even unit quantity.
If one confuses the contribution margin with the variable costs per unit, a wrong, too-low contribution ratio results and thereby a too-high calculated break-even sales figure.
A company should at least achieve enough sales that all costs are covered; only beyond that does the profit zone begin that secures its existence in the long run.
Because fixed costs are €4,000,000, break-even sales are also €4,000,000, independently of the contribution ratio.
At break-even sales, after deducting variable costs exactly the fixed costs remain; profit at this point is zero.
tactical_explanations:
Both paths meet the same quantity. Fixed costs divided by unit contribution margin and the detour via sales (fixed costs by ratio, then by the price) are mathematically equivalent. The unit quantity at which the sum of contributions reaches the fixed costs is accordingly the same. Deviations signal calculation errors, not a second truth.

The statement is true.

If one wrongly puts variable costs instead of the contribution margin in the numerator of the ratio calculation, a too-low contribution ratio results. Because break-even sales equal fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio, a too-low ratio in the denominator leads to a too-high calculated sales figure.

The statement is true.

Below cost coverage existence room is missing. In the long run a company cannot exist if revenues do not cover costs. The break-even point marks this minimum threshold; only sales above generate profit and financial room. The statement correctly links threshold and long-term securing. Proximity alone does not suffice.

The statement is true.

Four million fixed costs are not automatically four million break-even sales. Only at a contribution ratio of 100 percent would both be identical. At every lower ratio sales must be larger. Equating ignores the ratio completely and is therefore false. The denominator of the formula is missing in the claim.

The statement is false.

At break-even, after quantity costs exactly the fixed-cost amount remains. The contribution margin achieved corresponds to the fixed costs; profit and loss are zero. Every additional sales euro above contributes to profit. That is accordingly the defining property of the point. The statement describes exactly this zero-profit situation. Every euro of sales above then contributes to profit for the first time.

The statement is true.

title: Marketing is more than advertising
context: Evaluate the following statements on the concept of marketing:
statements: Marketing is the systematic orientation of the entire company — that is, of all operational areas — and of its offering to the needs and wishes of customers.
Marketing consists mainly of advertising and otherwise hardly concerns the rest of the company.
If a company produces past the market and its offering is not demanded, it cannot cover its costs, runs into payment difficulties and fails.
In a market economy, orientation to the market is secondary for business success, because demand will adapt to the finished offering anyway.
The common assumption that marketing is mainly advertising falls short.
tactical_explanations:
All areas, not only the advertising department. Theory defines marketing as the systematic orientation of the entire company — that is, of all operational areas — and of its offering to the needs and wishes of customers. Planning, production, price, distribution and sales all belong to it. Anyone who narrows marketing to posters and spots describes exactly the common assumption that theory rejects. Without this alignment to customer wishes, the offering remains a chance product. Anyone who only reorganises the communications department and leaves production and sales untouched has not yet oriented the whole company to the market and therefore does not meet the definition.

The statement is true.

Advertising alone does not carry the concept. The common assumption that marketing is mainly about advertising is expressly rejected. Marketing is the systematic orientation of the whole company and its offering to customer needs. Advertising messages are later only one part of communication policy. A firm that only advertises but produces past the market does not cover its costs. Narrowing the term to advertising makes the statement false.

The statement is false.

A shortfall in demand leads to payment problems. If a company produces past the market and its offering is not demanded, it cannot cover its costs, runs into payment difficulties and fails. In a market economy, market orientation therefore decides survival, not the good will of production. Anyone who denies the link between missing demand and failure contradicts this chain.

The statement is true.

The market does not wait for the finished warehouse. Orientation to the market is decisive for a company in a market economy. If the offering does not match need and wish, it sits unsold and costs remain uncovered. The idea that demand will simply adapt to what was built internally reverses the logic: first clarify customer needs, then align the offering. Theory does not claim that market orientation is secondary.

The statement is false.

The shortcut advertising equals marketing does not hold. Contrary to the common assumption that it is mainly about advertising, marketing is the systematic orientation of the entire company and its offering to the customer. Advertising remains a small part of communication policy. The statement captures exactly this correction without declaring advertising unimportant.

The statement is true.

title: Tasks of successful marketing
context: Evaluate the following statements on the tasks of successful marketing:
statements: For successful marketing, a company must find out what existing and potential future customers need and wish for.
The offering may be set internally independently of the ascertained customer wishes.
Once the product is finished, communication of the benefit may be omitted, because good goods sell themselves.
Prices must be designed so that customers can and want to demand the offering.
Whether the offering is available at the right place at the right time plays no role for successful marketing.
tactical_explanations:
Existing and future customers both count. Successful marketing begins by finding out what existing and potential future customers need and wish for. Market research supplies fundamental information for that. Anyone who asks only today's regular buyers and ignores potential buyer groups shortens the first task. Clarifying need is the starting point, not an optional add-on after production. Without that clarification, price, place and message remain a blind flight, because nobody knows whose need the offering is meant to meet.

The statement is true.

Internal setting without reference to wishes breaks the sequence. After needs have been clarified, the company's offering must be planned accordingly. A programme decided internally independently of the ascertained wishes is exactly producing past the market. The second task of successful marketing would then be missed. Planning follows need, not the other way round.

The statement is false.

Unknown goods stay in the warehouse. Successful marketing includes communicating offering and benefit to customers so that they learn about them. The bicycle example is clear: if the bikes are good and affordable but nobody knows them because nowhere are they pointed out, little is sold either. The claim that communication is superfluous once quality is right contradicts this step.

The statement is false.

Price must enable demand. Prices must be designed so that customers can and want to demand the offering. If they cannot afford the price or will not pay it, an otherwise matching product sits unsold. Price design is therefore a task of its own in successful marketing, not merely an internal cost calculation without regard to willingness to pay.

The statement is true.

Place and timing belong to the task. Successful marketing organises that the offering is available at the right place at the right time. Distribution is decisive, because even a right product at the wrong place cannot be sold. Anyone who declares availability secondary strikes exactly this fifth point. Without a matching sales channel, the benefit remains theoretical.

The statement is false.

title: Four areas and the product concept
context: Evaluate the following statements on market-oriented questions and on the product in marketing:
statements: Marketing measures relate especially to product and assortment policy, price and terms policy, distribution policy and communication policy.
In marketing, only tangible goods such as a bicycle or a pack of crystal sugar count as a product.
Services, organisations, campaigns, ideas, persons and places can be marketed and count as a product in marketing.
A fitness studio, a tax consultancy or a tutoring institute do not practise marketing, because they do not manufacture a tangible good.
If advice, training and ongoing support are offered around a product, the product in the marketing sense comprises both the thing itself and the related services.
tactical_explanations:
Four questions bundle the measures. What is offered, at what price, where, and with what message to whom: marketing measures relate especially to that — in marketing language Product, Price, Place and Promotion. Product programme and assortment, prices and terms, sales organisation, as well as advertising, sales promotion and public relations belong to it. Anyone who counts only one of these blocks as marketing shortens the market-oriented questions. Market research supplies the fundamental information for exactly these four questions so that the areas are not decided independently of one another.

The statement is true.

Tangibility is not a prerequisite. In marketing language, not only tangible things such as a bicycle or a pack of crystal sugar are called a product. Services, organisations, campaigns, ideas, persons and places can be marketed and also count as a product. Restricting the term to goods one can take in hand contradicts this extension. A tutoring institute then markets a product just as a bike manufacturer does.

The statement is false.

This point: the extended product concept is explicit. Services, organisations, campaigns, ideas, persons and places can be marketed and count as a product in marketing. Aid organisations, parties, initiatives, cities, regions and countries accordingly practise marketing. The statement reproduces this list without declaring every arbitrary topic an already marketed product; what matters is that it is an offering aligned to needs.

The statement is true.

Service providers are not outside. A service company such as a fitness studio, a tax consultancy or a tutoring institute also practises marketing. The examples stand in the theory precisely because marketing is not tied to manufacturing tangible goods. Anyone who denies these businesses marketing reverses the extension of the product concept.

The statement is false.

Additional services belong to the marketed bundle. Offering advice, training and ongoing support around a product means that the product in the marketing sense comprises both the thing itself and the related services. Product and assortment policy therefore also relates to additional services, not only to the core object. A bike without training can then be a different marketed product from the same bike with support.

The statement is true.

title: Price, distribution and communication
context: Evaluate the following statements on price, distribution and communication policy:
statements: Price and terms policy includes, besides the level of prices, also discounts, promotions and special prices as well as delivery and payment terms.
Especially with food, many buyers mainly take the cheapest offering.
A right product at the wrong place can still be sold reliably, because distribution is secondary.
Advertising is only a small part of a company's overall marketing.
Communication policy is limited to classic advertising and excludes sales promotion as well as public relations.
tactical_explanations:
Terms are more than the list price. Marketing measures in the price area relate to the level and design of prices, to discounts, promotions and special prices, and to delivery and payment terms. Anyone who thinks of price policy only as the final amount on the sign leaves out discount, promotion and payment period, although they are expressly included. Willingness to pay often hangs exactly on these terms. A promotional price without a payment period or a list price without discount policy would therefore be only a slice of the same price and terms policy.

The statement is true.

Food purchase often follows the cheapest offering. With many products, customers react mainly to price. Especially with food, many buyers mainly take the cheapest offering; willingness to pay more for a high-quality product is often limited. The statement captures this observation without claiming that quality never plays a role.

The statement is true.

The wrong place stops even a matching product. Distribution policy organises sales so that products reach customers, for example via wholesale and retail, the internet, branches, franchising or sales agents. Distribution is decisive, because even a right product at the wrong place cannot then be sold. Treating the sales channel as secondary contradicts exactly this point.

The statement is false.

Advertising does not carry all of marketing. Communication policy comprises advertising, sales promotion and public relations. Advertising is therefore only a small part of overall marketing. That connects to the definition that marketing is the orientation of the whole company, not the sum of advertisements.

The statement is true.

Sales promotion and PR belong to it. Communication policy relates to advertising, sales promotion and public relations. Anyone who excludes sales promotion and public relations drops two of the three named blocks. Classic advertising remains one part, not the whole message policy. The restriction makes the statement false.

The statement is false.

title: Market orientation across the whole company
context: A bicycle manufacturer aligns offering, price, distribution and notices to parents and children. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: Some understand marketing not only as a management process but as a philosophy for the entire company that orients itself to the market and to the company environment.
Marketing mainly concerns the advertising department and leaves planning, development and distribution largely untouched.
If bicycles are produced that parents or children do not like, that do not ride well, that are too expensive or that are only awkwardly available, the company cannot sell its products.
If the bikes are good and affordable, they sell reliably even when nobody points them out.
Marketing measures should be used not only case by case or phase by phase, but continuously and systematically coordinated with one another.
tactical_explanations:
Philosophy reaches beyond the process. Marketing concerns many company areas, from planning and developing the offering through production to distribution and sales. Some understand it beyond that as a philosophy for the entire company that orients its actions to the market and to the company environment. The statement reproduces exactly this second reading without striking the process view.

The statement is true.

Marketing orients the entire company to the market — far beyond advertising.

The statement is false.

Appeal, riding, price and availability help decide. If the manufacturer does not orient itself to the needs of parents and children, sales fail: bikes that are not liked, do not ride well, are too expensive or are only awkwardly available cannot be sold. The example bundles product, price and distribution. The statement captures the scene without isolating each single feature as the sole exclusion criterion; together they make a sale unlikely. If one of these links is missing, good will in the workshop is not enough: the market then does not take the bike, and costs remain uncovered.

The statement is true.

Invisible quality stays invisible. If the products are good and affordable but nobody knows them because nowhere are these bikes pointed out, little is sold either. Communicating the benefit belongs to successful marketing. The claim that pointing them out is superfluous once quality and price are right contradicts the example.

The statement is false.

Coordination is an ongoing task. The measures should not be used only case by case or phase by phase, but continuously and systematically coordinated with one another. This coordination is not always easy; data from market research help in making the right decisions. Anyone who only provides campaign islands without ongoing coordination misses exactly this requirement.

The statement is true.

title: Aligning product, price, place and message
context: A high-quality bicycle is to be perceived as exclusive and of high quality. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: A high price is interpreted by many buyers as an indicator of quality and exclusivity.
If the bike is too cheap, many will doubt the quality or no longer consider it exclusive.
If the bike is too expensive, potential buyers may yet buy another bike.
If the high-quality bike is offered in many shops, including less specialised ones, exclusivity remains untouched.
Product and price must be well aligned with each other, as must place of availability and the marketing message.
tactical_explanations:
Price often signals quality. A high-quality bicycle has a high price because production was expensive and quality is high; comparable bikes lie similarly. A high price is interpreted by many buyers as an indicator of quality and exclusivity. Signal and actual quality must fit together. If the price lies clearly below comparable high-quality bikes, exactly this signal tips, even though the product itself was expensive to produce.

The statement is true.

Too cheap undermines the quality presumption. If the bike is too cheap, many will doubt the quality or no longer consider it exclusive. The price must fit the product, otherwise perception tips. A dumping price for an allegedly high-quality bike contradicts the alignment of Product and Price. Theory describes exactly these doubts.

The statement is true.

An excessive price drives buyers to alternatives. If the bike is too expensive, potential buyers may yet buy another bike. A high price as a quality indicator therefore has an upper limit in willingness to pay. Product and price must therefore be well aligned.

The statement is true.

Wide scattering dilutes exclusivity. If the bike is offered in many shops, including less specialised ones, in order to reach as many customers as possible, it is likewise no longer considered exclusive. The place of sale carries the positioning with it. Anyone who claims exclusivity remains untouched ignores exactly this example. Specialist shops and mass shelves send different signals. Anyone who wants to keep exclusivity must also consider the sales channel; mass shelves and specialist shops do not send the same quality promise.

The statement is false.

Four levers must fit together. Product and price must be well aligned, as must the place where the product is available and the message with which it is marketed. Advertising and other sales-promoting measures should awaken the wish to buy exactly this bike and no other. Isolated optimisation of one quantity destroys the alignment.

The statement is true.

title: Goals of marketing measures
context: Evaluate the following statements on marketing goals:
statements: Most marketing measures aim to reach the target group, that is, exactly the persons one wants to address with the offering.
A frequent goal is a high degree of awareness and a positive image, where appropriate an image correction.
Possible marketing goals are to retain existing customers and to win new customers.
Holding or increasing sales as well as covering costs or making a profit do not belong among possible marketing goals.
With retained and newly won customers, the share of the overall market can be held or increased.
tactical_explanations:
The target group is the common core. Marketing goals are varied. What most measures share is that they should reach the target group, that is, exactly the persons one wants to reach and address with the offering. Scattering without this group of persons misses the common denominator. Measures that stick with quite different persons can spread awareness and still miss the intended target group.

The statement is true.

Awareness and image belong to the shared goals. Besides reaching the target group, the shared goals name a high degree of awareness and being seen positively, or an image correction. Anyone who admits only sales figures as a goal drops this block. Awareness without a positive image would be incomplete; correction presupposes that the previous image does not fit. Image correction presupposes that the target group's previous image does not match the offering; awareness alone does not heal a negative image. Being seen positively and being known are therefore two connected but not identical goals of the same measures.

The statement is true.

Retaining and winning stand side by side. Further possible marketing goals consist in retaining existing customers and winning new customers. Both aim at the customer base, not only at one-off first purchases. Anyone who counts only new customers and ignores regulars, or the reverse, shortens the list. The statement captures both sides.

The statement is true.

Sales and cost coverage stand on the same list. Further possible goals are to hold or increase sales and thereby at least cover costs or make profits. The claim that these quantities do not belong among marketing goals strikes exactly this continuation. Market orientation should ultimately carry economically, not only send messages.

The statement is false.

The customer base supports market share. Retaining existing customers and winning new ones is meant to hold or even increase the share of the overall market. Market share is here the bridge between customer work and position in the overall market. The statement follows this chain without declaring market share the only goal.

The statement is true.

title: Marketing concept and customer satisfaction
context: Evaluate the following statements on the marketing concept:
statements: A comprehensive marketing concept orients itself to the market, sets precisely formulated goals and coordinates all measures of market orientation, in particular Product, Price, Place and Promotion.
Such a concept should lead to customer satisfaction, which is the prerequisite for business success.
Price policy concerns only the list price; discounts, promotions as well as delivery and payment terms do not belong to it.
Customer satisfaction is irrelevant for business success according to the theory.
The concept is developed in order to achieve the marketing goals.
tactical_explanations:
Market, goals and the four areas belong together. A comprehensive marketing concept is developed in order to achieve the marketing goals. It orients itself to the market, sets precisely formulated goals and coordinates all measures in the company that serve market orientation, in particular Product, Price, Place and Promotion. If one of these elements is missing, the concept is not the comprehensive one described. Coordination means alignment, not parallel isolated actions. Without coordination, a high price and mass distribution can contradict each other even though each instrument seems justified on its own.

The statement is true.

Satisfaction carries success. Such a concept should lead to customer satisfaction, which is the prerequisite for business success. Without fulfilled needs, sales remain fragile even if short-term revenue arises. The statement establishes the link: concept, satisfaction, success. Satisfaction is here a condition, not merely a soft extra. Dissatisfied buyers carry neither repeat purchases nor the market share that further marketing goals aim for.

The statement is true.

Price and terms policy also includes discounts, promotions and terms.

The statement is false.

Success hangs on satisfaction. Customer satisfaction is expressly the prerequisite for business success. Irrelevance would deny this prerequisite. The concept is meant to lead there precisely because dissatisfied customers do not carry the offering. The statement reverses this relationship.

The statement is false.

Goals are the reason for the concept. A comprehensive marketing concept is developed in order to achieve the marketing goals. It is the instrument, not an end in itself beside the goals. Orientation to the market and coordination of measures serve the same achievement. The statement captures this purpose.

The statement is true.

title: The market concept in marketing
context: Evaluate the following statements on the market and on market research:
statements: In general, the market denotes the meeting of supply of and demand for a particular good.
In marketing, market means the sum of persons and/or companies that have a need which can be fulfilled with the product offered.
Distribution policy mainly means the advertising message with which customers are addressed.
Among other things, market research supplies the fundamental information for the market-oriented questions.
The market is secondary for the alignment of marketing measures.
tactical_explanations:
The general definition remains supply meets demand. While the market in general denotes the meeting of supply of and demand for a particular good, marketing uses a narrower, need-related concept. The statement holds the general side. Without supply and demand there would be no such market concept; it is the starting point before marketing language rephrases.

The statement is true.

Marketing counts need-holders, not only transactions. In marketing, market means the sum of persons and/or companies that have a need which can be fulfilled with the product offered. That also includes those who do not yet buy but whose need could be fulfilled. Market potential later builds exactly on that. The statement reproduces this definition.

The statement is true.

Distribution concerns sales channels and availability (Place), not the communication message (Promotion).

The statement is false.

Market research feeds the four questions. A company orients its offering to market-oriented questions for which, among other things, market research supplies the fundamental information. Without these data, coordination of measures remains uncertain. The statement captures the supporting function without equating market research with all of marketing.

The statement is true.

Alignment needs the market. The market is essential for the alignment of marketing measures. Secondary status contradicts this point and all of market orientation. Goals, concept and indicators presuppose clarity about which market is meant. Anyone who strikes the market leaves the measures without a reference point.

The statement is false.

title: Market potential and market volume
context: Evaluate the following statements on market potential and market volume:
statements: Market potential is the maximum possible sales quantity of a product.
Market volume is the quantity of the product actually sold.
If market volume lies close to market potential, the market is almost saturated.
Market potential and market volume are the same amount, because every need-holder already buys.
Saturated markets are often turned back into unsaturated markets through changed products or by addressing new buyer groups.
tactical_explanations:
Maximum of all conceivable purchases. Market potential is the maximum possible sales quantity of a product. It makes clear how large a market would be if all persons and/or companies that have a need which could be fulfilled with the product actually bought that product. The figure is therefore an upper limit, not a booked actual quantity. Anyone who equates potential with today's sales misses exactly this maximum. If volume lies clearly below it, room remains; if it lies close to it, hardly any additional sales in the existing market are possible.

The statement is true.

Actual sales of all suppliers. Market volume measures the quantity of the product actually sold, not the theoretical maximum. The difference from market potential shows unused room. Anyone who swaps volume and potential confuses actual and upper limit. The statement holds the actual figure. Only the difference from potential shows the unused room.

The statement is true.

A narrow gap means saturation. If market volume lies close to market potential, hardly any additional sales to the same need-holders are possible. Almost all reachable buyers then already buy. A wide gap would mean unsaturated. Proximity of the two figures is the saturation signal. A wide gap between the two figures would by contrast mean unsaturated.

The statement is true.

Equality is the border case, not the rule. Potential is the maximum quantity, volume the actual. They coincide only if really all with a fulfilable need buy. The claim that they are always the same amount because every need-holder already buys treats saturation as the normal case. The terms are separated precisely because that often does not hold.

The statement is false.

New models or new groups open the market. Often attempts are made to turn saturated markets back into unsaturated markets through changed products or by addressing new buyer groups, for example through new models with new functions. Then the relevant potential or demand rises above previous volume. New functions or new age groups shift who has a fulfilable need and thus the gap between volume and potential.

The statement is true.

title: Sales potential, sales volume and market share
context: Evaluate the following statements on company-related sales indicators:
statements: Sales or sales potential of a company denotes the sales quantity that the company can reach in the best case or hopes to reach.
Sales or sales volume is a company's sales for a particular product or product group.
A company's market share for a product can be determined in quantity or in value terms.
Sales potential and market potential denote the same figure: the maximum possible sales quantity of the overall market.
The sales potential of woom GmbH is the sales quantity of bicycles that it can sell in the ideal case.
tactical_explanations:
Best case of the company's own quantity. Sales or sales potential of a company for a product or product group denotes the sales quantity that the company can reach in the best case or hopes to reach. That is the company-related upper limit, not the market potential of all suppliers. Hope and best case mark that it is not the sales already realised. Market potential remains the upper limit of all suppliers; one firm's sales potential can lie below it, because not every company can serve the whole market.

The statement is true.

Actual sales of the company's own firm. Sales or sales volume is a company's sales for a particular product or product group. At company level it corresponds to what market volume is at market level: the quantity actually sold, here only of the one firm. The statement separates this actual figure from potential.

The statement is true.

Quantity or value are both admissible. A company's market share for a product can be determined in quantity or in value terms. Unit counts and revenues can therefore carry the same share idea, but at different prices lead to different percentages. Theory allows both routes. Anyone who recognises only one of the two calculation methods shortens the indicator.

The statement is true.

Market potential relates to the overall market; sales or sales potential means the quantity reachable by the individual company.

The statement is false.

woom illustrates the best case. Sales potential is the quantity that the company can sell in the ideal case, not today's sales. The example makes the company-related upper limit concrete. Between potential and actual volume lies the company's own growth room. The statement captures exactly this best-case figure. Between potential and actual volume lies the company's own growth room.

The statement is true.

title: Absolute and relative market share
context: A bicycle manufacturer turns over 15 million euros, market volume is 100 million euros, the largest competitor turns over 30 million euros. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: Absolute market share gives the share of company revenue in market volume and is calculated as company revenue times 100 divided by market volume.
Relative market share relates company revenue to the revenue of the largest competitor.
A relative market share greater than one indicates that the company is the market leader.
In the numerical example the absolute market share is 15 percent.
In the numerical example the relative market share is 2; the company is therefore market leader.
tactical_explanations:
The formula ties revenue to market volume. Absolute market share gives the share of company revenue in market volume. Computationally: company revenue times 100, divided by market volume. That produces a percentage of the entire actual market, not a comparison only with one rival. Anyone who puts the largest competitor in the denominator is already calculating the relative share and misses the absolute formula.

The statement is true.

The reference point is the largest competitor. Relative market share relates company revenue to the revenue of the largest competitor. The denominator is therefore not market volume but the strongest rival. That produces a ranking indicator, not a percentage of the overall market. The statement captures this relation.

The statement is true.

Above one means ahead. A relative market share greater than one indicates that the company is the market leader, because its own revenue exceeds that of the previously largest competitor. Equal to one would mean a tie with the largest; below one would mean lagging behind. The threshold of one is the rule for leadership in this indicator.

The statement is true.

Fifteen divided by one hundred times one hundred. Absolute market share = company revenue × 100 / market volume = 15 × 100 / 100 = 15. The manufacturer therefore holds 15 percent of value market volume. Fifteen divided by 30 would be a different calculation and would concern the relative share. The 15 percent follow solely from revenue and volume.

The statement is true.

Fifteen divided by thirty is one half. Relative market share = company revenue / revenue of the largest competitor = 15 / 30 = 0.5. That is smaller than one, so not market leader. The claim that the relative share is 2 reverses numerator and denominator (30 / 15 = 2 would be the rival's lead). 0.5 shows lag versus the largest, even though 15 percent absolute is already a noteworthy chunk of volume.

Note: Absolute 15 percent and relative 0.5 can coincide; the one figure does not replace the other. Absolute 15 percent describes the chunk of total volume; relative 0.5 describes the lag versus the largest. Both figures are needed, because the one does not replace the other.

The statement is false.

title: Market segmentation
context: Evaluate the following statements on dividing the market into buyer groups:
statements: It is usually not sensible to develop products for the overall market and to practise marketing for every product on all markets.
The market is divided into buyer groups that comprise persons with commonalities in particular characteristics, for example age, income or consumption habits.
Through segmentation, product development, prices, sales channels and advertising can be aligned more purposefully.
Target groups are primarily the persons who demand and buy products; influencers and users who do not buy do not count among them.
Needs and buying behaviour of the various buyer groups are so similar that a division is dispensable.
tactical_explanations:
The overall market for every product overstretches. Needs and buying behaviour of the various buyer groups are very different. Therefore it is usually not sensible to develop products for the overall market and to practise marketing for every product on all markets. Undifferentiated scattering misses the differences. The statement reproduces this starting critique. A children's bike for all age and income groups at once would fail on exactly these differences; that is why one divides the market. More purposeful prices and sales channels presuppose that these groups have been formed beforehand.

The statement is true.

Characteristics bundle groups. The market is divided into buyer groups (target groups), segmented. Each group comprises persons with commonalities in particular characteristics, for example age, income, consumption habits. Homogeneity relates to these characteristics, not to complete identity of all persons. The statement captures definition and examples.

The statement is true.

More purposeful instruments follow the division. Thereby one can align product development, prices, sales channels and advertising more purposefully. Segmentation is therefore a means to more fitting market cultivation, not an end in itself. Without division the four areas remain coarse. The statement holds this benefit.

The statement is true.

Target groups also include influencers of the purchase decision and users who do not buy themselves.

The statement is false.

Differences are the reason for division. Needs and buying behaviour are very different; that is why one segments. The claim that the groups are so similar that division is dispensable reverses the premise. Uniform marketing for the overall market would then again be the rejected solution.

The statement is false.

title: Target groups beyond buyers
context: Parents buy a children's bike, the child rides it, friends recommend the model. Evaluate the following statements:
statements: Persons who influence the purchase decision can also belong to the target group of marketing activities.
Persons who do not buy but use the product can also belong to the target group.
Only those who pay the purchase price come into consideration as a target group.
The child who uses the bike without paying itself can be a target group.
Because friends can influence the decision, the company may forgo any segmentation and cultivate all markets equally.
tactical_explanations:
Influencers count in the circle. Target groups are not only demanders and buyers, but also those who influence the purchase decision. Friends who recommend a model belong in this wider circle. Marketing that sees only the paying person misses recommendations that first trigger the purchase. A campaign that sees only the paying person leaves recommendations and usage wishes aside even though they trigger the purchase. Buyers, influencers and users are named side by side, not as a ranking in which only the paying person counts.

The statement is true.

Use without purchase remains relevant. The target group also includes those who do not buy but then use the product. Satisfaction and wish often arise with the user while another person pays. Anyone who blanks out users plans past usage.

The statement is true.

Payers alone are too few. The list names buyers, influencers and users. Admitting only persons who pay the purchase price strikes two of the three roles. Parents pay, children use, friends influence: all three can be a target group. Narrowing to the payer makes the statement false.

The statement is false.

Use without paying can be a target group. The child rides the bike while the parents buy and pay. Product design and message must therefore not ignore the user role. Target group comprises more than only the paying person. The scene deliberately separates buyer and user. Buyer role and user role are deliberately to be separated in the target group.

The statement is true.

Several roles do not replace the division. Different buyer groups remain the reason to segment. That friends influence widens the target group but does not cancel the statement that it is usually not sensible to advertise equally for the overall market and on all markets. Forgoing segmentation contradicts market cultivation in three phases. Segmentation remains necessary because age, income and consumption habits still form groups with different buying behaviour.

The statement is false.

title: Three phases of market cultivation
context: Evaluate the following statements on the phases of target-group-oriented marketing:
statements: In the first phase the market is segmented, in the second it is decided which market segments are to be cultivated, in the third the company positions its offering on this target market.
Positioning of the offering takes place before segmentation of the market.
Positioning describes how the product is seen or is to be seen by consumers with regard to important properties.
After segmentation the company cultivates every segment formed with the same marketing measures.
The target market on which positioning takes place results from the selection of the segments to be cultivated.
tactical_explanations:
Three steps in fixed order. Target-group-oriented marketing proceeds in three phases: first the market is segmented, then it is decided which market segments are to be cultivated, thereafter the company positions its offering on this target market. Selection follows division, positioning follows selection. Anyone who reverses the order misses the phase scheme. If one skips selection, one positions in the unfiltered overall market and misses the point of the second phase.
